articles.title: How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?
articles.summary: The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy explains how it happened, and what it means for you.
articles.body:
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports.

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy gets a political education in a grueling Ohio governor’s race
articles.summary: Holding a town hall Saturday in the second least populous county in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy seemed further than ever from the presidential campaign trail where...
articles.body:
Holding a town hall Saturday in the second least populous county in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy seemed further than ever from the presidential campaign trail where he made his political debut three years ago.

President Donald Trump barely came up. The war in Iran wasn't mentioned.

Instead, Ramaswamy fielded multiple questions in Monroe County, along the Ohio-West Virginia border, about how he would pay for the property tax cuts he's promising if he's elected, which he touts as the largest such rollback in state history.

"There are some things that are out of control of a governor, and I'm not going to give you just some fake promise," Ramaswamy said at one point.

The biotech entrepreneur is attempting a rare route in politics, going from national notoriety as a presidential candidate to running for state office. And he's making his pivot during an election cycle where headwinds are blowing against all kinds of Republicans.

On top of it all, he's trying to convince an overwhelmingly White, Christian and middle-class state to make him its first Indian American governor, first Hindu governor and first billionaire governor.

It has not been easy. Even though Trump endorsed him early on, Ramaswamy has had to weather Republican second-guessing. He's drawn a Democratic opponent in Amy Acton, Ohio's former public health director, who refuses to debate him, saying she will not platform a "serial liar." Polls show the contest remains close even though his campaign and allied groups have poured over $120 million into advertising in the state, more than triple the spending on Acton's side.

The race took an explosive new turn Monday after video circulated onlin e showing Acton's estranged mother calling her a liar and urging Ohioans to oppose her. Acton and her brother denounced the video, while Ramaswamy's campaign said Ohioans "deserve to know" the mother's message, even as it declined to say whether it had any involvement in the video.

It all amounts to a herculean effort to muscle Ramaswamy through in a state that Trump won by 11 percentage points in 2024 — and it has come with a political education for the Cincinnati native.

"I think he's learned some things as you travel around the state, particularly a state like Ohio that's so big and diverse," said Terry Casey, a Republican strategist in Ohio. "Learning all those nuances, talking with elected officials at the local level, you see and hear things and realize some of the realities."

Ramaswamy acknowledges he does not fit the profile of a typical Ohio statewide candidate. His contest is in direct contrast with the Senate race, where two candidates with decades of experience in Ohio politics, GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, are duking it out in another tight campaign.

"I'm a businessman," the 41-year-old Ramaswamy said Sunday at the Darke County GOP Hog Roast, speaking amid a parade of mostly older, White candidates already working in Columbus. "I'm not somebody who has grown up in Ohio politics. I'll be the first person to admit that. I don't have experience in Ohio government. A lot of the men and women you're hearing from today do, and we're going to rely on them. … But for my part, I'm an outsider."

Speaking with CNN afterward, Ramaswamy said he has come to appreciate how impactful a governor can be, even if it is "not in ways that are part of the national cultural zeitgeist." He pointed to property taxes, saying they have moved from a "top-five issue" for him to a "top-one issue."

Democrats say Ramaswamy has come off as elitist and out of touch, pointing to his private jet travel between campaign events. One of Acton's latest ads shows Ramaswamy joking about being "dirty rich" in an old TV interview.

Yet Ramaswamy's allies say he's running an energetic campaign against the odds.

"It's a tough environment," Sen. Bernie Moreno told CNN after Ramaswamy spoke Sunday at the Miami County GOP Picnic. "I think if we had $2-a-gallon gas … he'd win by 20 points. So you can't separate what's happening at the national level from just what's happening, what's going to happen on the ballot. But ultimately Vivek, I think, will win."

On the day of Trump's second inauguration in January 2025, Ramaswamy announced he would not join Elon Musk at the newly created Department of Government Efficiency as initially expected. A month later, Trump endorsed Ramaswamy on the day he announced his campaign.

Top Ohio Republicans were slow to consolidate behind him. Then-Attorney General Dave Yost kept his own gubernatorial campaign going for about another three months, dropping out after the state GOP endorsed Ramaswamy. Lt. Gov. Jim Tressel, the championship-winning former Ohio State football coach, kept open the possibility that he could run until that September.

Outgoing GOP Gov. Mike DeWine withheld his endorsement until this January, bestowing it after Ramaswamy named state Senate President Rob McColley as his running mate.

Ramaswamy ended up drawing a May primary challenge from a little-known automotive engineer, Casey Putsch, who pitched himself as more of an everyman and leaned into ethnic grievances, suggesting Ramaswamy had contempt for "American cultural values." Putsch received 18% of the vote and has refused to back Ramaswamy.

Ramaswamy stands out as a practicing Hindu in a state where 64% of adults identify as Christian, according to a Pew Research Center Religious Landscape Study. Ramaswamy listened along Sunday in Darke County as a pastor led a prayer for Republican candidates to "submit" themselves to God.

Aaron Baer, the president of the Center for Christian Virtue in Columbus, said he backed Ramaswamy early partly to show the nominee was an ally of Christians. Baer said there were "a lot of us who were concerned" in those early days, but it no longer feels like a source of tension.

"There's always the online trolls and there's that kind of stuff, but actually on the ground, it's gone so well," Baer said.

Former state Rep. Jena Powell, who previously represented a solidly red district in rural western Ohio, said she has been "all in" on Ramaswamy and urged fellow Republicans to unify.

"People have, you know, different ideas of who they may have wanted as governor," Powell said, "but as I tell every Republican, the primary is over, we have Vivek and we want to have him as our Republican governor."

Ramaswamy's blue-collar appeal was under the spotlight Saturday in Monroe County, a working-class GOP stronghold in the heart of Appalachia. He was introduced by a fellow statewide candidate from the region, Jay Edwards, who acknowledged they "come from two different worlds" and "wealth classes."

"I'm going to hold his feet to the fire," Edwards said, "but I don't think he's going to need it."

Ramaswamy's message there resonated with one attendee, Chris Wilson, who said he was a coal miner for over a decade and now works in an industry that is being hurt by Trump's tariffs on Canada. Ramaswamy seems to be for "blue-collar America," Wilson said.

"If that's who he's willing to help, then I don't care what walk of life he comes from," Wilson said. "I'm interested in what his policies are and what that's going to do for us."

Ramaswamy is not running to the center. He's promising to be the "most conservative" Ohio governor ever. And Ramaswamy, whose 2021 book "Woke Inc." birthed his political rise, still rails against "transgenderism" and "climate-ism."

But even then, he's run into the realities of governing versus campaigning. He's faced questions about how he plans to fund public education and other state services under his plans to bring down property taxes and phase out the state income tax.

Ramaswamy also caused a stir earlier this year when he suggested shutting down some public colleges in Ohio to help fund a reduction in the income tax. He avoided repeating that when asked about it Saturday, but generally promised to make tough decisions to address declining enrollment.

"If there's one person who will save our higher education system in Ohio, it's me," he said.

Casey, the strategist, said the episode was an example of how Ramaswamy has started with a "broad brush" in some policy areas and refined them as he has grown as a candidate.

Ramaswamy has also had to respond to growing voter concerns about data centers, issuing a proposal in August to block any new projects unless they meet three conditions, including that they provide free electricity to nearby residents. Acton has proposed her own "conditional" data center moratorium and highlighted past comments by Ramaswamy where he called the proliferation of data centers in Ohio "a good thing."

Nick Owens, a self-described lifelong Republican who runs the anti-data center group Conserve Ohio, said he has seen Ramaswamy evolve on the issue.

"There's definitely a greater awareness to how hyperscale data center developments are affecting rural Ohioans to Vivek," Owens said. "I think he was looking at it as a pure economic development lens and didn't really quite grasp the impact on everyday Ohioans and many Ohioans which make up the MAGA base."

Ramaswamy seldom went out of his way to tie himself to Trump while stumping over the weekend, another contrast with his presidential bid, where he lavished praise on Trump even while running against him.

Some distance could be helpful in the midterms. After watching Ramaswamy speak in Miami County, a local GOP activist, Tom Matthew, said he has "reservations" with some Trump policies these days but found Ramaswamy to be "fresh air."

In Acton, Ramaswamy has an especially galvanizing opponent for Ohio Republicans due to her leading role in the state's Covid-19 shutdowns. They refer to her as "the Anthony Fauci of Ohio." In Darke County, a life-size cutout of Acton wearing a mask awaited Republicans at the end of the dessert line.

Acton has generally defended her record and made a point of noting she was working under a Republican governor in DeWine, who earlier this year defended her against a Ramaswamy ad claiming she decided to delay Ohio's primaries in 2020. And she's also appealed to independents and Republicans by breaking with her party on issues such as transgender athletes' participation in sports.

But her decision not to debate Ramaswamy has proven especially animating for Republicans and fueled the perception she is running a more buttoned-up campaign. Ramaswamy mentioned her refusal to debate no fewer than a dozen times throughout the weekend.

In a statement for this story, Acton said Ramaswamy "isn't just out of touch, he's out for himself."

"It's no surprise the only people who would benefit from his plans are billionaires like him," she said.

As Ramaswamy campaigned across three solidly Republican counties this weekend, a handful of voters said they were firmly opposed to Acton but still coming around on Ramaswamy. One of them, Charlene Pickerill-Bowman, said she walked into the Darke County hog roast undecided on Ramaswamy and left a supporter.

Another woman, Darla Medal, said she was "leaning toward" Ramaswamy after hearing his bold campaign promises in Monroe County.

"If he can do it all, that would be great," she said. "I just think that it's been bad lately, the last couple of years. I think the Democrats (have) put us there and the Republicans are going to have to pull us out, hopefully — hopefully — and it just depends on who's going to do it."

articles.title: 'Pêndulo' eleitoral, MG espelha divisão entre direita e esquerda | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio Bolsonaro venceu no 1° turno no total de votos no estado, enquanto Lula liderou em número de municípios. Resultados para Senado e Câmara também revelam forças de direita e esquerda no eleitorado mineiro.
articles.summary: As eleições em Minas Gerais mostram um estado dividido entre Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula, consolidando o peso de MG como termômetro da disputa nacional.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: REUTERS/Diego Vara e REUTERS/Adriano Machado

O resultado do primeiro turno das eleições expôs as diferentes forças políticas que convivem em Minas Gerais: Republicanos e PL, do campo da direita, e PT, da esquerda, conquistaram as principais vitórias nas urnas, nas disputas por governo e Senado e pelas vagas de deputados.

Considerado por estudiosos um "estado pêndulo", por oscilar entre direita e esquerda nos últimos 30 anos, Minas apresenta hoje uma clara divisão em seu eleitorado.

Apontado também como “espelho do Brasil” por refletir o resultado nacional das eleições presidenciais desde a redemocratização, o estado reproduz a atual divisão observada na disputa nacional entre Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

O cenário reforça a importância de Minas Gerais no segundo turno, e o estado está no foco das campanhas de Flávio e Lula nos últimos dias. Nesta quarta-feira (21), Lula participou de um ato no Centro de BH. Na semana passada, ele esteve em Juiz de Fora, na Zona da Mata, e em Ipatinga, no Vale do Aço. Flávio foi a Capelinha, no Vale do Jequitinhonha, e deve ter ato com apoiadores em BH no sábado (24). Entenda ao fim da reportagem o motivo da escolha dessas cidades.

Esse reflexo do Brasil pode ser analisado a partir dos seguintes pontos, que são detalhados ao longo desta reportagem :

Flávio Bolsonaro venceu no 1° turno no número total de votos no estado, enquanto Lula liderou no maior número de municípios.

Na votação de 4 de outubro, os eleitores mineiros escolheram para o Senado um representante do PL, Domingos Sávio, e uma representante do PT, Marília Campos.

Na Câmara dos Deputados , a bancada do PL se tornou a maior de Minas, repetindo o cenário nacional – foram 21 representantes. Apesar disso, entre os 10 deputados federais mais votados no estado, 5 são do PT, contra 2 do PL ( leia mais abaixo sobre a composição da Câmara e do Senado ).

Entre os eleitos para a Câmara, estão alguns dos principais mobilizadores das campanhas de Flávio e Lula . De um lado, Nikolas Ferreira (PL) , mais votado do país, aliado do candidato da direita e empenhado na corrida de Flávio ao segundo turno. Do outro, a segunda mais votada e mulher mais jovem eleita na Câmara, aos 21 anos, Ana Elisa (PT) se tornou importante referência na corrida lulista para o segundo turno, ao lado do deputado reeleito André Janones (Rede) .

A eleição para o governo de MG não representou uma divisão equilibrada como nas outras escolhas dos eleitores mineiros, pois o governador eleito, Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos) , venceu no primeiro turno com 55,4% dos votos, com diferença de quase 30 pontos percentuais em relação ao segundo colocado. Por outro lado, mesmo alinhado a Flávio Bolsonaro, ele defendeu uma das principais pautas atuais da esquerda e bandeira de Lula: o fim da escala 6 x 1 no Senado . Ele chegou a afirmar que foi o responsável por fazer Flávio mudar de ideia sobre o tema, tendo o senador presidenciável dado voto favorável à PEC que acaba com escala 6 x 1.

Minas Gerais teve no primeiro turno índice de abstenção maior que o percentual do Brasil e tem o segundo maior colégio eleitoral do país , com 16,3 milhões de eleitores, atrás apenas de São Paulo.

Entenda a divisão entre direita e esquerda em Minas Gerais a partir dos seguintes aspectos:

Foco das campanhas presidenciais e 22% de abstenção

Os fatos descritos acima ajudam a explicar por que Minas entrou no centro das campanhas presidenciais no segundo turno. Enquanto Lula busca a virada no estado, Flávio quer ampliar a vantagem.

Embora o nome do PL tenha garantido a liderança em MG em 4 de outubro , o petista venceu na maioria dos municípios mineiros. O candidato à reeleição ficou na frente em 452 cidades, e o adversário, em 401.

Entre os focos dos candidatos estão os 3.735.098 eleitores que não foram às urnas no primeiro turno. O índice de abstenções no estado (22,8%) superou o do Brasil (21,08%) .

"Desde a redemocratização, o estado sempre votou no candidato que venceu a eleição presidencial. Por isso, tem peso eleitoral e também simbólico: o resultado mineiro costuma ser tratado como um termômetro da disputa nacional", explica Felipe Nunes, diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV).

O primeiro turno terminou com Flávio Bolsonaro em vantagem no Sul de Minas , no Triângulo Mineiro, no Alto Paranaíba e na Região Central. Lula conquistou a liderança no Norte, Jequitinhonha, Mucuri e também na Zona da Mata (veja mapa mais abaixo) .

Conforme apontam estudiosos, em termos econômicos, sociais e territoriais, o Sul tem forte integração com São Paulo; o Triângulo, com Goiás e Distrito Federal; o Norte de Minas tem características semelhantes às do Nordeste brasileiro; e a Zona da Mata recebe influência do Rio de Janeiro.

Apesar de Lula ter vencido em mais municípios do que Flávio, o candidato do PL encerrou o primeiro turno com 588.612 votos a mais do que o petista no estado.

Entre os dez maiores colégios eleitorais de MG, Flávio liderou em nove: Belo Horizonte, Uberlândia, Contagem, Betim, Montes Claros, Uberaba, Ribeirão das Neves, Governador Valadares e Ipatinga. Lula ganhou apenas em Juiz de Fora.

No resultado total das urnas no estado, Flávio obteve 48,24% dos votos, e o petista, 43,33%. Augusto Cury (Avante) ficou na terceira posição, com 3,42%, seguido por Renan Santos (Missão), com 2,06%, e Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), com 1,92%. O ex-governador de Minas Gerais, Romeu Zema (Novo), terminou em sexto lugar, com 0,82% dos votos.

Em todo o Brasil, Flávio Bolsonaro ficou com 47,03% dos votos; Lula, com 45,16% . Na sequência apareceram Cury (2,89%), Renan (2,24%), Caiado (2,18%) e Zema (0,27%).

Infográfico mostra resultados das eleições presidenciais em MG no 1º turno — Foto: Kayan Albertin - Arte/g1

Enquanto a votação presidencial deixou Minas dividida, a disputa pelo governo foi definida no primeiro turno. O senador Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos) foi eleito governador com 55,40% dos votos válidos .

O candidato de Lula, Patrus Ananias (PT), ficou em segundo lugar, com 26,34%, e o candidato de Flávio Bolsonaro, Flávio Roscoe (PL), em terceiro, com 6,97%.

A candidatura de Patrus foi definida depois que outras alternativas defendidas pelo PT para a disputa não avançaram. Antes dele, houve uma tentativa de viabilizar o nome do senador Rodrigo Pacheco (PSB), que descartou disputar a eleição e anunciou que deixaria política , e o de Marília Campos (PT), que recusou candidatura ao governo e concorreu ao Senado, tendo sido eleita.

Já Flávio Roscoe foi lançado pelo PL em meio à indefinição sobre a candidatura de Cleitinho, que liderava as pesquisas de intenção de voto para o governo de Minas. O PL tentou construir uma candidatura unificada da direita em torno do senador, mas decidiu lançar candidatura própria com Roscoe depois que o Republicanos demorou a viabilizar o nome de Cleitinho .

A candidatura de Cleitinho foi marcada por muitas idas e vindas. O senador chegou a recuar e declarar que não concorreria , antes de ter o nome confirmado pelo Republicanos em agosto.

O político trabalhou como verdureiro no sacolão da família, mas foi como músico que começou a ficar conhecido em Divinópolis, sua cidade natal. Em dez anos, de 2016 a 2026, ele foi eleito vereador, deputado estadual, senador e, por fim, governador.

Em discurso, à tribuna, senador Cleitinho (Republicanos-MG). — Foto: Carlos Moura/Agência Senado

Cleitinho prometeu revisar as isenções fiscais, conceder reajustes anuais aos servidores públicos e reduzir o Imposto sobre a Propriedade de Veículos Automotores (IPVA) . Ele também afirmou que pretende negociar a dívida de Minas com o governo federal, independentemente de quem ocupe a Presidência da República.

O governador eleito declarou apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro, embora tenha divergido publicamente do presidenciável . Cleitinho era defensor do fim da escala 6x1, uma das principais pautas atuais da esquerda e bandeira de Lula, enquanto o candidato do PL criticou a proposta durante toda a tramitação.

No entanto, em 14 de outubro, Flávio Bolsonaro votou a favor da PEC que acaba com a escala 6x1 . Em entrevista, Cleitinho chegou a dizer que foi o responsável por fazer Flávio mudar de ideia.

Minas Gerais elegeu senadores do PL e do PT . Domingos Sávio (PL) foi o mais votado, com 4.968.829 votos (24,21%). Marília Campos (PT) ficou com a segunda vaga, com 3.990.864 votos (19,44%).

Sávio já foi deputado estadual e, atualmente, está no quarto mandato como deputado federal. Ele será senador pela primeira vez, com apoio de Flávio Bolsonaro.

Marília participou da fundação do PT na região do Triângulo Mineiro, na década de 1980. Ela já foi deputada estadual e eleita quatro vezes prefeita de Contagem, na Grande BH. Apoiada por Lula, também ocupará uma cadeira no Senado pela primeira vez.

A disputa pela Câmara Alta ainda tinha nomes como o atual senador Carlos Viana (PSD), que ficou na terceira posição, com 17,46% dos votos, e o ex-governador de Minas e ex-senador Aécio Neves (PSDB), que acabou em sétimo lugar, com 4,08%.

O PL conquistou 21 das 53 cadeiras de Minas Gerais na Câmara dos Deputados . A Federação Brasil da Esperança, formada por PT, PCdoB e PV, ficou com 13. União Brasil e PP, reunidos na Federação União Progressista, conquistaram seis. O Republicanos elegeu três deputados federais.

A lista dos dez candidatos mais votados do estado, no entanto, teve outro desenho. O primeiro colocado foi Nikolas Ferreira (PL), que se tornou o deputado federal mais votado da história do país com 3.119.318 votos. Ele é um dos principais aliados de Flávio na corrida presidencial.

Na sequência, apareceu Ana Elisa (PT), com 524.219 votos. Aos 21 anos, ela se tornou a mulher mais votada da história de Minas Gerais para a Câmara e a deputada federal mais jovem eleita no país desde pelo menos 1994 . Ana tem participado ativamente da campanha de Lula, principalmente nas redes sociais.

A lista dos dez mais votados inclui ainda outros quatro candidatos do PT – Reginaldo Lopes, Rogério Correia, Ana Pimentel e Gleide Andrade –, além de Duda Salabert (PSOL), Pinheirinho (PP), Zé Vitor (PL) e Weliton Prado (PSD).

Quem não aparece na lista, mas também ganhou protagonismo na campanha de segundo turno, é André Janones (Rede), deputado federal reeleito com 78.780 votos. Ele é o responsável pelo canal de WhatsApp "Exército do Lula" , que nesta quarta-feira (21) alcançou a marca de mais de 7 milhões de seguidores.

Como MG votou para a Assembleia Legislativa

Na Assembleia Legislativa de Minas Gerais (ALMG), o PL saltou de 13 para 21 cadeiras . O partido terá a maior bancada na Casa a partir de 2027.

O PT aparece logo atrás, com 15 deputados, seguido pelo PSD, com nove. PP terá cinco parlamentares, e Republicanos, quatro.

Bruno Engler (PL) foi o estadual mais votado, com 675.940 votos. Beatriz Cerqueira (PT) ficou em segundo lugar, com 328.402.

Campanha presidencial de 2º turno em Minas

O estado que se dividiu nas urnas virou também um dos principais focos das campanhas dos presidenciáveis.

Lula voltou a Minas em 16 de outubro. Primeiro foi a Juiz de Fora , a única das dez maiores cidades mineiras onde ficou à frente de Flávio Bolsonaro no primeiro turno. Depois, seguiu para Ipatinga, onde o candidato do PL obteve vantagem de 29 pontos percentuais.

Nesta quarta-feira (21), o petista participou de uma caminhada em Belo Horizonte . Ele estava acompanhado de aliados como o ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira, e a senadora eleita Marília Campos.

Atos de apoio a Lula também têm sido registrados em diferentes cidades do estado desde o início da campanha de segundo turno.

Já Flávio Bolsonaro escolheu outro ponto estratégico para a primeira visita a MG nesta etapa. Em 15 de outubro, ele esteve em Capelinha, no Vale do Jequitinhonha , uma das poucas cidades da região onde venceu Lula no dia 4.

No próximo sábado (24), véspera da eleição, ele deve visitar a capital mineira, ao lado de aliados como Nikolas Ferreira e Cleitinho Azevedo.

articles.title: Lula diz ao TSE aceitar condições, mas quer dados de empresa de Willer | G1
articles.standfirst: Já a campanha de Flávio afirma que vai analisar resposta de Lula antes de tomar uma medida e que, se sigilo do petista for divulgado, Deltan Dallagnol analisará o material.
articles.summary: Lula aceita abrir sigilos no TSE, mas exige que Flávio Bolsonaro inclua dados da empresa Alcazar Holdings para garantir a transparência total entre as partes.
articles.body:
Em manifestação apresentada nesta quarta-feira (22) no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), a defesa do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva registrou que o petista "não se opõe a absolutamente nada" quanto à abertura de seus sigilos bancários, fiscais e telefônicos.

No entanto, Lula afirmou que o desafio original proposto por ele deve ser cumprido em sua totalidade , insistindo para que a campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) inclua na divulgação de sigilos os dados da empresa Alcazar Holdings, sediada na Ilha da Madeira e de propriedade do advogado Willer Tomaz , apontado como amigo próximo do adversário.

No documento enviado ao ministro André Mendonça , Lula diz que a régua da transparência deve ser a mesma para ambos os lados.

A petição de Lula diz que a Polícia Federal encontrou registros indicando que Flávio figurava como "usuário master" da conta da Alcazar em um banco privado , vínculo que teria sido desfeito apenas em maio de 2025, após o início da Operação Sem Desconto, que apura fraudes no INSS .

O texto também menciona viagem de Flávio em um jato executivo da empresa de Willer Tomaz . "Se, como [o candidato do PL] afirma, nada tem a esconder, não há razão para que a conta da Alcazar fique fora das gavetas que ele mesmo propôs abrir. Quem não deve, não recorta", diz a petição do presidente.

Do outro lado, a defesa e os aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro reagiram à movimentação. A advogada da campanha, Maria Cláudia Bucchianeri, declarou que o grupo irá analisar o que Lula apresentar antes de protocolar os próprios dados .

"Nós pedimos que o sigilo não seja de 8 anos. Precisamos dar um passo além, Lula está no poder há 20 anos. Precisamos saber o padrão de vida do casal presidencial. A gente precisa verdadeiramente de uma transparência. Queremos os telefones que eram usados", afirmou Bucchianeri.

Aliado de Flávio, o ex-procurador da Lava Jato Deltan Dallagnol foi "escalado" pela campanha do candidato do PL para analisar os documentos de Lula, caso os sigilos sejam quebrados:

"Lula é especialista em ocultar patrimônio. Última vez que analisei o sigilo de Lula ele foi parar na cadeia", declarou Dallagnol em referência à prisão de Lula determinada pelo ex-juiz Sergio Moro em 2018 .

A proposta defendida por Lula é de que ambos os candidatos realizem um protocolo conjunto e simultâneo no TSE, apresentando de forma integral os termos de quebra de sigilo para garantir ampla publicidade ao eleitor brasileiro.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: veja quando acabam os comícios e a propaganda eleitoral | G1
articles.standfirst: Comícios e impulsionamento de propaganda na internet terminam nesta quinta-feira (22). Horário eleitoral gratuito vai até sexta (23), e caminhadas e carreatas são permitidas até sábado (24).
articles.summary: Comícios e impulsionamento terminam nesta quinta (22); horário eleitoral acaba na sexta (23), e caminhadas e carreatas podem ocorrer até sábado (24).
articles.body:
Fiscais do TRE-AM observaram quatro ocorrências de propaganda eleitoral irregular neste fim de semana em Manaus. — Foto: Júnior Souza/TRE-AM

A três dias do segundo turno das eleições de 2026, marcado para domingo (25), as campanhas eleitorais entram na reta final para a realização de atos e divulgação de propaganda política.

De acordo com o calendário do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), esta quinta-feira (22) é o último dia para a realização de comícios e para a circulação de propaganda eleitoral paga ou impulsionada na internet.

Quinta-feira (22) : último dia para comícios e impulsionamento de propaganda eleitoral na internet.

Sexta-feira (23) : fim do horário eleitoral gratuito no rádio e na TV, dos anúncios pagos na imprensa escrita e dos debates entre candidatos.

Sábado (24) : último dia para caminhadas, carreatas, passeatas e distribuição de material gráfico, até as 22h.

Domingo (25) : segundo turno das eleições, com votação das 8h às 17h, pelo horário de Brasília.

🤳🏽 Quinta-feira (22): comícios e impulsionamento na internet

Esta quinta-feira é o último dia para a realização de comícios e uso de equipamentos de som em locais fixos para transmitir discursos e mensagens de campanha aos eleitores.

Os eventos podem ocorrer entre 8h e meia-noite. No caso do comício de encerramento da campanha, a legislação permite a prorrogação por mais duas horas, até as 2h da madrugada de sexta-feira (23).

Também termina nesta quinta-feira o prazo para circulação de propaganda eleitoral paga ou impulsionada na internet. A proibição vale mesmo para anúncios contratados anteriormente, que deverão deixar de circular.

🎙️Sexta-feira (23): horário eleitoral e debates

A sexta-feira será o último dia de exibição da propaganda eleitoral gratuita no rádio e na televisão relativa ao segundo turno.

Também termina o prazo para a divulgação paga de anúncios eleitorais em jornais e revistas impressos, assim como para a reprodução desses anúncios na internet, respeitados os limites previstos na legislação.

O dia marca ainda o prazo final para a realização de debates eleitorais no rádio e na televisão, que não poderão ultrapassar a meia-noite.

🚶🏽‍♂️Sábado (24): caminhadas, carreatas e distribuição de santinhos

Na véspera do segundo turno, as campanhas ainda poderão realizar caminhadas, carreatas e passeatas, acompanhadas ou não por carros de som ou minitrios.

A distribuição de material gráfico, como santinhos e panfletos, também será permitida. Essas atividades deverão ser encerradas até às 22h de sábado (24).

O segundo turno das eleições será realizado no domingo (25), com votação para presidente e vice-presidente da República e, onde houver, governador e vice-governador .

A votação ocorrerá das 8h às 17h, pelo horário de Brasília.

No dia da eleição, são proibidos atos de campanha, como comícios, carreatas e a distribuição de material de propaganda eleitoral .

O eleitor, no entanto, pode manifestar individualmente e de forma silenciosa sua preferência política, por meio de bandeiras, broches, adesivos e camisetas.

A divulgação dos resultados da votação terá início a partir das 17h, conforme o calendário da Justiça Eleitoral.

articles.title: Campanha de Lula intensifica busca de votos entre beneficiários do Bolsa Família que ainda votam em Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.body:
A campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) intensificou, nesta reta final da eleição, a busca por votos entre os beneficiários do Bolsa Família.

Segundo assessores da campanha petista, esse é o principal grupo no qual Lula ainda teria espaço para conquistar eleitores que hoje declaram voto no senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), seu adversário no segundo turno.

A avaliação da equipe de Lula é que, nos demais segmentos, os votos estão mais consolidados e há menos espaço para mudança até domingo (25), dia da votação.

Segundo apurou o blog , a campanha de Lula está entrando em contato, por meio de mensagens, com beneficiários do Bolsa Família.

A estratégia é destacar o reajuste do benefício concedido pelo governo Lula e lembrar declarações antigas de Flávio Bolsonaro, que, no passado, chamou o programa de "Bolsa Farelo".

"Neste grupo, o Lula está conquistando mais votos e pode crescer mais, tirando votos de Flávio Bolsonaro", diz um interlocutor do presidente.

Programa Bolsa Família — Foto: Divulgação/MDS

O Bolsa Família se tornou um dos principais temas da reta final da disputa presidencial. Lula tem usado o programa para tentar ampliar sua vantagem entre os eleitores de menor renda, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro tem afirmado que não pretende acabar com o benefício.

A proposta apresentada pela equipe de Flávio é aumentar o período de transição para beneficiários que consigam emprego formal ou abram um negócio e, por isso, passem a deixar o programa. ​

Na pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21), Lula oscilou positivamente entre os eleitores que recebem benefícios sociais, como o Bolsa Família, de 60% para 62%, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro oscilou negativamente, de 31% para 27%.

O levantamento mostra ainda que a rejeição de Lula, que ficou em 47% no conjunto dos entrevistados, é menor entre os beneficiários do Bolsa Família: 27%. Já a rejeição de Flávio Bolsonaro, de 52% no total, chega a 68% nesse grupo.

No cenário geral da pesquisa Quaest, Flávio aparece com 45% das intenções de voto, e Lula, com 44%. Como a margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos, os dois estão tecnicamente empatados.

O levantamento ouviu 2.154 eleitores entre 17 e 20 de outubro e foi registrado no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

O objetivo da campanha de Lula é tentar chegar a 70% de apoio entre os beneficiários do Bolsa Família. Se atingir esse patamar, a equipe do presidente, que tenta a reeleição, acredita que terá condições de virar a disputa até domingo.

Além dos beneficiários do Bolsa Família, a campanha de Lula também está buscando eleitores que não compareceram às urnas no primeiro turno ou que votaram em branco ou anularam o voto.

A campanha escalou lideranças regionais para entrar em contato com esses eleitores e tentar convencê-los a votar em Lula na reta final.

A estratégia mira um grupo relevante para o resultado: segundo a Quaest, entre os eleitores que afirmam não ter comparecido ou ter votado em branco ou nulo no primeiro turno, 40% dizem que agora pretendem votar em Lula e 36%, em Flávio Bolsonaro. ​

As devidas liberações devem ser enviadas ao TSE até às 23h59 desta quinta-feira, segundo o acordo.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) em agenda de campanha na quarta-feira (21/10) — Foto: Montagem/g1

No entanto, Lula afirmou que o desafio original proposto por ele deve ser cumprido em sua totalidade, insistindo para que a campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) inclua, na divulgação de sigilos, os dados da empresa Alcazar Holdings, sediada na Ilha da Madeira e de propriedade do advogado Willer Tomaz, apontado como amigo próximo do adversário.

A petição de Lula diz que a Polícia Federal encontrou registros indicando que Flávio figurava como "usuário master" da conta da Alcazar em um banco privado, vínculo que teria sido desfeito apenas em maio de 2025, após o início da Operação Sem Desconto, que apura fraudes no INSS.

O texto também menciona viagem de Flávio em um jato executivo da empresa de Willer Tomaz. "Se, como [o candidato do PL] afirma, nada tem a esconder, não há razão para que a conta da Alcazar fique fora das gavetas que ele mesmo propôs abrir. Quem não deve, não recorta", diz a petição do presidente.

No início desta tarde, Camilo Santana, que integra a campanha do petista, leu para a imprensa o documento que prevê o acordo.

"A abertura será imediata, total, nas condições integrais aceitas por ambos, e simultânea para os dois candidatos. Os dados relativos às autorizações já apresentadas, próprias, de familiares, e de empresas, serão abertos e divulgados hoje, 22.10.2026", prossegue.

O texto requer que o ministro Mendonça determine, "ainda hoje, a requisição de dados ao Banco Central do Brasil, às instituições financeiras, à Receita Federal e às operadoras de telefonia, e sua divulgação simultânea no DivulgaCandContas ou em outro sítio eletrônico de acesso público".

O documento é assinado pelo presidente Lula e por Maria Claudia Bucchianeri, coordenadora da equipe jurídica da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro.

articles.title: Em sessão, Estela Aranha relata sobrecarga no TSE e diz despachar até 50 processos por dia | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministra afirmou que chegou a assinar voto às 2h59 para manter ritmo de trabalho; eleição presidencial já registra mais de 800 ações no tribunal.
articles.summary: Ministra afirmou que chegou a assinar voto às 2h59 para manter ritmo de trabalho; eleição presidencial já registra mais de 800 ações no tribunal.
articles.body:
A ministra do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) Estela Aranha relatou nesta quinta-feira (22), durante sessão da Corte, a sobrecarga de trabalho provocada pela judicialização da campanha eleitoral.

Segundo a ministra, seu gabinete despacha uma média de 40 a 50 processos por dia e, nesta semana, ela chegou a assinar um voto às 2h59 da manhã para tentar manter o ritmo de trabalho.

A declaração foi dada durante a discussão sobre a possibilidade de terceiros que se considerem prejudicados por propaganda eleitoral recorrerem à Justiça Eleitoral.

Inicialmente, Estela demonstrou preocupação com o impacto que a ampliação dessa possibilidade poderia provocar na quantidade de processos ( entenda mais abaixo ).

"A minha preocupação, na verdade, é uma questão processual, de terceiros que estão fora do processo eleitoral começarem a ingressar de modo massivo na Justiça Eleitoral para pedir algum tipo de retratação, e isso inviabilizaria", afirmou.

Ao argumentar sobre a sobrecarga dos gabinetes, Estela citou o ritmo de trabalho às vésperas do segundo turno.

"Ontem, até a minha equipe, que não está aqui, estava reclamando que o meu último voto foi assinado às 2h59 da manhã para tentar manter o ritmo."

A ministra afirmou ainda que o volume de processos tem reflexos também no trabalho da Procuradoria, que precisa se manifestar sobre os casos.

"Eu estou mandando uma média de 40, 50 processos por dia", disse.

Ministra Estela Aranha. — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE/Divulgação

Estela afirmou que faltam recursos para responder à demanda e classificou o cenário como de "judicialização excessiva".

O relato ocorre no momento em que o TSE enfrenta um volume recorde de processos relacionados à disputa presidencial.

Até a noite desta quarta (21), o tribunal havia recebido ao menos 804 ações, mais que o dobro das 325 registradas no mesmo período da eleição de 2022. Em 2018, foram 388 no período.

As representações eleitorais tratam de questões do dia a dia da campanha, como propaganda irregular e pedidos de retirada de publicações, e são julgadas por juízes auxiliares.

Ao longo da campanha, as ações passaram a tratar de temas como divulgação de fatos inverídicos, impulsionamento de conteúdo negativo contra candidatos e propagandas veiculadas no rádio e na televisão.

O TSE também precisou analisar questões envolvendo canais de WhatsApp e o uso de deepfakes.

No caso analisado nesta quinta, Estela sustentou em seu voto que não seria possível estabelecer uma legitimidade ampla para que terceiros alheios ao processo eleitoral recorressem ao TSE.

A ministra argumentou que a abertura dessa possibilidade, especialmente em uma eleição presidencial, poderia comprometer a capacidade da Justiça Eleitoral de dar respostas aos processos sobre propaganda.

Estela afirmou ainda que a pessoa que se sentir prejudicada poderia buscar a Justiça comum para discutir eventual dano à honra, inclusive com a possibilidade de pedir uma reparação que não poderia ser concedida pela Justiça Eleitoral.

No caso em julgamento, segundo a ministra, a propaganda questionada havia sido exibida apenas no dia 10 de outubro, uma vez pela manhã e outra à noite. A ação foi apresentada no dia seguinte, quando, segundo Estela, a peça já havia deixado de ser veiculada.

Ela afirmou também que procura promover conversas e conciliações com as campanhas para evitar novos processos e que, nesse caso, havia o compromisso de não voltar a veicular a propaganda.

O tema provocou divergências durante a sessão.

O ministro André Mendonça reconheceu a sobrecarga de trabalho durante o período eleitoral, mas ponderou que esse cenário não poderia simplesmente afastar a possibilidade de um terceiro que se considere prejudicado buscar uma providência na Justiça Eleitoral.

Dias Toffoli também defendeu a legitimidade de terceiros. O ministro argumentou que entregar exclusivamente à Justiça comum a discussão sobre a imagem de uma pessoa em propaganda poderia trazer problemas de competência.

Depois dos argumentos apresentados durante o debate, Estela chegou a afirmar que revia seu entendimento para admitir a chamada legitimidade extraordinária do terceiro prejudicado.

"Em vista desses argumentos apresentados agora pelo ministro [Dias] Toffoli e pelo eminente relator, eu revejo meu voto para convergir no sentido de admitir que haja essa legitimidade extraordinária do terceiro prejudicado", disse.

Estela considerou ainda uma solução a possibilidade de desfocar a imagem da pessoa que aparecesse indevidamente na propaganda.

Segundo ela, não se trataria propriamente de direito de resposta, mas de uma providência prática para impedir uma nova exposição.

No entanto, ao fazer posteriormente a leitura formal de seu voto, Estela voltou a sustentar a tese de que não deveria haver uma legitimidade ampla para terceiros acionarem o TSE, defendendo que a pretensão fosse levada à Justiça comum.

A ministra encerrou o voto defendendo que não se abrisse essa legitimidade "ampla" para todos aqueles que eventualmente se sentissem prejudicados por uma propaganda.

Estela critica decisões da Justiça comum sobre campanha

Durante a discussão, Estela fez ainda um alerta sobre outro problema que, segundo ela, tem ocorrido "com frequência": a atuação da Justiça comum em questões relacionadas à propaganda eleitoral.

A ministra afirmou ter tomado conhecimento de decisões da Justiça Federal em Brasília e do Tribunal de Justiça do Rio de Janeiro relacionadas a campanhas nacionais.

Segundo Estela, há casos em que uma mesma questão chega à Justiça Eleitoral e à Justiça comum, o que pode resultar em decisões diferentes sobre um mesmo assunto.

"Têm partes que simplesmente pegam o mesmo processo e protocolam no TRF e no meu gabinete, por exemplo. E aí eu vou dar a decisão. Já tem uma decisão sobre o mesmo assunto no TRF1. E como é que eu vou dar uma decisão divergente? Como nós vamos equacionar isso?", questionou.

Estela afirmou que a situação precisa ser discutida pelo tribunal.

"Se a competência e a atribuição é do TSE, e em especial em campanhas nacionais, não podem tanto a Justiça Federal quanto a Justiça estadual estarem tomando decisões referentes às campanhas nacionais porque as partes acham que vão ter mais facilidades nas decisões", declarou.

A ministra disse ainda que há casos em que as partes recorrem a mais de um ramo do Judiciário em busca de uma decisão favorável.

Segundo ela, a questão extrapola o processo específico analisado nesta quinta e precisa ser tratada pela Corte para evitar decisões contraditórias.

A quantidade de processos já levou o TSE a tentar reduzir a judicialização entre as campanhas.

No último dia 13, após o primeiro turno, o tribunal reuniu representantes das campanhas de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro para discutir formas de reduzir a disputa judicial, além de medidas contra a desinformação e o uso indevido de imagem e voz por inteligência artificial.

Na ocasião, as duas campanhas concordaram em abrir mão de representações relativas à pré-campanha e de pedidos de direito de resposta relacionados ao primeiro turno.

articles.title: 5 takeaways from final Michigan U.S. Senate debate and what was said
articles.summary: With less than two weeks until the election, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers made their pitches to the voters of Detroit and across the state.
articles.body:
The second and final debate between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers in the race for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat on Wednesday, Oct. 21 saw each playing to the hometown crowd in metro Detroit, attempting to score partisan points, expand their base and frame their opponent as a far different kind of candidate than he and his allies let on.

El-Sayed, Rogers claimed, engaged in "a pattern of deception" over his real aims.

"They are trying to distract you," El-Sayed said of Rogers and the Republican's arguments against him.

And so it went for an hour-long debate at WXYZ-TV's Southfield studios outside Detroit as El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee and former Wayne County and Detroit health director, sparred with Rogers, a former Republican congressman.

Here's a handful of takeaways from this debate ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election.

Michigan's second and final debate for open U.S. Senate seat

There was plenty of back-and-forth arguing and no dearth of personal attacks in this debate, but compared to the one 13 days previous at WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids , it was far more polite.

Yes, there were times when the moderators had to remind one or the other of the time constraints and cut them off. And yes, there were plenty of harangues and invective, true or not.

But it definitely didn't seem as chippy as the scene in west Michigan, as if both were a little more willing to keep from fighting after the bell.

Making a pitch for Detroit and Democrats

It seemed both were acutely aware that this debate was intended for a Detroit audience and the importance of that big voting bloc to their hopes of winning.

Rogers tried to poke holes in El-Sayed's claims of building a statewide political coalition, noting he did not win Detroit in the August primary, a Democratic stronghold. (U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Birmingham, did, while losing statewide.) Rogers claims he's making inroads in the city. (His wife was recently handing out gas cards at an east side Detroit gas station, according to the Michigan Chronicle .)

But El-Sayed turned the Detroit attack around, saying voters in the city are tired of those questioning the legitimacy of election administration in the city like Rogers has.

El-Sayed said: "Folks in the city of Detroit are sick and tired of watching politicians deny the outcome of elections just like Mike has, just like Donald Trump has." And he dragged Rogers, presumably as a state legislator, as having helped create the emergency manager law that took some authority from Detroiters back in 2013 and remains a sore point in the city.

Rogers also talked up the coalition of Democratic voters he has built to paint his opponent as flailing to secure support from within his own party. And while it's clear some Democratic voters, particularly Jewish voters, are uncomfortable with El-Sayed and his harsh line on aid to Israel, it's far from clear how large that group is (and whether it's not linked to Republican efforts).

Major Democrats have backed El-Sayed, including Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and former President Barack Obama, who is coming into Detroit for him on Saturday, Oct. 24.

Early and often throughout the debate, Rogers characterized El-Sayed as being aligned with the policies and priorities of the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA. And repeatedly, El-Sayed tagged Rogers as an ally — referring to him during the debate as a "sock puppet" — of President Donald Trump, a supporter of his policies and having only gotten in the race to replace retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters because Trump asked him to do so.

El-Sayed isn't a DSA member, he's made that clear. He does share some policy goals, like enacted universal, government-run health care and cutting military aid to Israel, with that group. But he also says he is a capitalist, one who wants more competition between business, not less.

As for Rogers, he had defended — or at least failed to criticize — Trump's positions on tariffs and on the war in Iran until recently, and is now being accused of flipflopping.

El-Sayed argued several times that Rogers and Republicans were playing "MAGA bingo" with their talking points, which were intended to distract voters from problems like the economy and high inflation.

Rogers said El-Sayed just wanted to connect him with Trump. "This is really about America," he said.

Asked if he plans to attend an upcoming Trump rally on Sunday, Oct. 25, Rogers told reporters: "I don't even know all the details."

During the debate El-Sayed claimed that Rogers invited Trump, telling Rogers he is "embarrassed of the fact that you cannot win this race without Donald Trump coming here and stumping for you. That's why you begged him to come."

Rogers made his recent point on tariffs, especially as they regard Canada, again, saying the trade war with Michigan's neighbor needed to end after having previously defended it.

He also partially defended Trump's tariffs again, arguing it had been good for the auto industry in some cases (while in fact, it's been a decidedly mixed bag with auto parts makers losing jobs over the last year.)

El-Sayed again argued in favor of tariffs, but not in the unilateral and sweeping manner used by Trump.

The two candidates also argued over Social Security, which is expected to be unable to pay its debts as of 2032, with Rogers repeating an unproven Republican claim that rooting out fraud could help stabilize it and El-Sayed arguing that taxing the wealthy could provide enough funding to right its finances, when it would likely take more than that.

Meanwhile, Rogers blasted El-Sayed's push for universal health care, Medicare-for-All, saying it would destroy Medicare as we know it and take away people's health care; as a practical matter, there is no evidence it would do either, though it likely would mean (El-Sayed's claims aside) that people with private or employer-sponsored health care would not have the same plans they do now. (Instead, they would likely fall under the Medicare-for-All plan if implemented.)

Also, during a yes/no answer on whether either supported expanding the U.S. Supreme Court: Rogers said, "no." El-Sayed said "yes, but fairly." Asked for the same yes/no response on whether either supported universal background checks for firearm purchases: El-Sayed said "yes," Rogers said, "It depends."

As expected, Rogers attempted to hammer El-Sayed again as having donors "from Hamas, Hezbollah," with no clear evidence supporting that or that El-Sayed has any link to those or any other groups advocating political violence, as the Free Press has previously reported.

"We need to know, are you for America or these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers said. "That is a risk to our national security."

El-Sayed, meanwhile, called out Rogers' changing stance on the Iran war and noted Trump's weekend appearance in Michigan, suggesting the two remain in lockstep, despite Rogers' claims of independance.

"They are hip-to-hip on this war, and you are paying the cost," he said.

And Rogers, who has recently called for a swift end to the war, which is driving up fuel prices and driving down Republican chances in the midterm elections, did seem to defend the decision to go to war with Iran.

"You want to pay $8 a gallon in gas? Let Iran get control of that region," Rogers said on the debate stage.

In closing, Rogers continued to paint his Democratic opponent as extreme.

"If you think about what's at stake in this election, it really isn't about left versus right anymore. It really is about the heart and soul of the country and who we are as Americans and the future we want for our children," he said.

El-Sayed ended by describing himself as a patriot concerned that cost-of-living challenges and corporate interests in politics have curtailed opportunity for Americans.

"Nobody appreciates the promise of America like somebody who understands exactly what America gave me," he said. "I love this country. I love the Constitution and what it protects for all of us. But right now, it has gotten way too hard."

Aaron Kall, director of debate at the University of Michigan, didn't think so, believing Rogers had a hard time giving succinct answers in the time allowed and El-Sayed "had an annoying habit of continually referring to his opponent as 'my guy.'"

"Much like their first contest, tonight's debate between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers was a heated exchange that mostly yielded a draw or split-decision that is likely unlikely to change the minds of many undecided voters," Kall said.

articles.title: Rubio, Hegseth point finger at Musk in Starlink slowdown
articles.summary: Top Trump administration officials are starting to point fingers squarely at SpaceX founder Elon Musk for the decision to slow down his company’s Starlink sa...
articles.body:
Top Trump administration officials are starting to point fingers squarely at SpaceX founder Elon Musk for the decision to slow down his company's Starlink satellite internet services and its military counterpart Starshield for Ukraine, which has been muddled in uncertainty over the culprit.

Looking to deflect the controversial move — which was swiftly admonished by powerful congressional Republicans and Democrats — Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said Ukraine's access to Starlink was up to Musk and not the White House.

"The bottom ​line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they'll allow it to be used at," Rubio told reporters while traveling to India.

And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking to reporters on Tuesday, suggested Starlink's slowdown was a commercial matter and not a result of any orders from the White House.

"There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions," Hegseth said.

Taken together, the comments are a change of tune from President Trump's original assertions last week that neither he nor Musk was responsible for the disruption. Rubio also on Saturday had insisted that no one ordered the slowdown.

The about-face comes after The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Musk ordered the slowdown of the satellite services, a vital tool Ukraine uses to defend itself from Russian missile and drone attacks.

Trump's role is unclear. The Journal reported that at least one person claimed Musk and Trump spoke prior to the slowdown. Reuters reported last week that the order to throttle Starlink came from inside the White House, in a directive to the Pentagon. Sources speaking to Reuters did not specify who at the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order.

"I don't know who did it but I was not involved," Trump told reporters Wednesday when asked.

Trump and Musk have experienced periods of fallout in their relationship but appear on the upswing today. A low point in their relationship occurred during a major public spat in June 2025, where Musk alleged that files on the disgraced financier and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein were kept secret to protect Trump.

But the relationship has rebounded since then. Trump awarded Musk the National Medal of Science earlier this month. And Musk has provided more than $276 million for Republicans in the midterm elections, The New York Times reported .

Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) on Wednesday said he doubted Trump had no hand in the slowdown, as he doesn't believe Musk "would do this without at least the acquiescence of the White House."

"I think it's frankly shameful," Cornyn said on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "I think we should be supporting the victim, not the aggressor."

Starlink's slowdown in Ukraine came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia and making a deal to purchase diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Zelensky called Trump "weak" for making the deal.

Part of Trump's response to Zelensky was to blame him as the obstacle to peace with Putin.

Republicans holding back blame on Trump for Starlink's throttling are demanding an investigation and accountability. Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.) have threatened to block Trump's agenda during the lame-duck session if answers are not provided.

"This is a very, very serious matter. It cannot be glossed over," Fitzpatrick told CNN on Tuesday, following the Journal report.

Fitzpatrick said if Musk ordered Starshield's slowdown, "that is likely a violation of the law."

"He has decisionmaking authority over Starlink, the civilian commercial product, but not Starshield, which is a military-grade national security tool. No individual civilian should have any decisionmaking authority over how that's deployed," he said.

Adding to the confusion, Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, has said Ukraine does not have access to Starshield.

"Starshield is a defense product ... the United States military uses," Rubio told reporters last week.

"It's not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that's under conversation. It's under discussion right now of how they would want to use it."

Zelensky on Tuesday said he discussed with Rubio "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored" and called the conversation "constructive" in a post on the social platform X .

Part of that conversation is whether the U.S. could give Ukraine the ability to hit targets deep inside Russia, in particular missile launchers, in exchange for halting Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.

Trump has demanded Ukraine halt strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that they are related to high diesel prices in the U.S., though they largely stem from the U.S. war against Iran.

Russia has refused to halt strikes against Ukrainian energy sites, in particular civilian electricity and heating infrastructure. Zelensky's allies in Congress have backed a proposal for the U.S. to give Ukraine the ability to hit Russian missile launchers in exchange for halting Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy facilities.

"President Trump can lower prices at the pump today by simply agreeing to this deal!" Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) wrote Sunday in a post on X. Wicker's pushback came after Trump announced he would buy Russian diesel to lower prices in the U.S.

Ukraine's ability to hit Russian launchers would rely on accessing Starlink inside Russia, where it's currently blocked. A bipartisan group of lawmakers — seven Republicans and 16 Democrats — wrote to Trump on Wednesday urging him to call Musk and give Ukrainians that access.

"With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," the lawmakers wrote.

"If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian 'arrows,' it must be able to shoot the 'archer.' The Starlink system run by Mr. Musk's company SpaceX could help with that."

articles.title: The 5 governor’s mansions most likely to flip in November
articles.summary: Three dozen governor’s mansions are on the ballot this fall, with several battleground contests that could shape national politics through the end of the second Trump administration. Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) forecast has Democrats favored in 21 of the 36 races, with a chance of flipping four GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Georgia…
articles.body:
Three dozen governor’s mansions are on the ballot this fall, with several battleground contests that could shape national politics through the end of the second Trump administration.

Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) forecast has Democrats favored in 21 of the 36 races, with a chance of flipping four GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Georgia — while Republicans could pull off their own flip in Kansas.

Some of those races could also mark a few firsts: If Democrat Amy Acton wins in Ohio, she’ll be the second woman to serve as governor of the Buckeye State but the first to win a full four-year term. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottom would be the first woman and first African American to serve as Georgia’s executive if she wins next month.

If Republican Vivek Ramaswamy won in Ohio, he’d become the first Indian American elected to the position and the first male Millennial to win a governor’s mansion. If Republican Rick Jackson wins in Georgia, it’s believed he would be the first billionaire elected governor in the state. And if Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins flips Alaska’s seat, he’d be the youngest governor in the Last Frontier’s history.

Here are the five governor’s mansions most likely to flip this fall:

Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited in a state that President Trump won by 16 points in 2024, which offers Republicans a likely pickup opportunity as Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson faces off against Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher.

The two candidates have tagged each other as “extreme” and “radical” at a Kansas State Fair debate last month, with Masterson attacking Holscher for changing her position on data center incentives. The pair have also tangled over addressing higher taxes, according to the Kansas Reflector .

Meanwhile, Holscher criticized her Republican opponent over abortion access in the state and has sought to tie Masterson to former Gov. Sam Brownback (R), whose time in the governor’s mansion was rocked by unstable state finances after he rolled back state taxes but offered no policies to bring in state revenue, according to the Kansas Reflector , prompting the state to punt projects and cut spending.

The president rallied in the Sunflower State on Monday as Senate race between Sen. Roger Marshall (R) and Democrat Adam Hamilton has turned into an unexpected battleground contest. Both Masterson and Marshall attended Trump’s rally in Park City, Kansas, where the president also announced a new $8-billion dollar Harvest Fuel Relief Program aimed at easing diesel costs for farmers.

A mix of Trump’s low approval ratings, high cost of living expenses and several controversies over Marshall’s spending and litigation against former patients have created a tighter than anticipated Senate contest.

While voters often differentiate candidates in statewide races compared to federal races – candidates typically toe party lines on federal candidates while usually being a little more open to crossing party lines in races for governor and other statewide elections – Marshall’s challenging reelection is an unhelpful dynamic for Masterson.

Cook Political Report rates the race as lean Republican. DDHQ gives Masterson a 69 percent probability of winning the seat, with his advantage narrowing in recent weeks.

Iowans haven’t elected a Democrat as governor in two decades, yet the party is feeling bullish about its chances of changing that next month in the race to replace outgoing Gov. Kim Reynolds (R).

Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand is facing off against Republican businessman Zach Lahn for the governor’s seat, with polling consistently showing Sand ahead. Sand has cast Lahn as a carpetbagger given the businessman, who co-founded a private school in Kansas, travels between the two states to see some of his children. The Kansas Reflector reported that Lahn voted in the Sunflower State as recently as 2022.

Lahn has said he travels to Kansas to be present in his children’s lives and has a “blended family.”

Sand has also touted his record in the state auditor’s office and has taken shots at both parties as he positions himself as a bipartisan public steward.

Lahn, who is supported by allies of the Make America Healthy Again movement for his focus on cancer rates and water quality, has rebuked Sand over his attacks on his travels to Kansas. He’s also attacked the Iowa auditor general over the family wealth of his wife, Christine Lauridsen Sand, the chief executive of Lauridsen Group. Lahn has invoked the culture wars, including tying Sand to transgender issues and has hit him on COVID-19 pandemic precautions taken to curb the spread of the virus.

Cook Political Report rates the race as lean Democratic. DDHQ gives Sand a 72 percent probability of winning, after a significant gain since the end of summer.

The Ohio governor’s mansion could flip for the first time in two decades as Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy tussle in an ugly fight for outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine’s seat.

The race took a turn this week after Ramaswamy elevated a video featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who urged Ohioans not to vote for the Democrat.

The ad was met with backlash as figures on both sides of the aisle argued it went too far, given Acton’s contentious history with her mother.

Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health under DeWine, has previously described a childhood plagued by abuse, neglect and rape at the hands of her stepfather, who pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury.

Experts saw the ad as an effort by Ramaswamy to make waves in the closing weeks of the tight campaign.

Acton has edged ahead in DDHQ’s latest polling averages, up by 3.4 percent over Ramaswamy. DDHQ rates it a coin-flip with Acton narrowly favored, giving the Democrat a 60 percent probability of a flip.

Cook Political Report also considers the race a toss-up, after shifting it away from Republicans this summer.

Democrats have been locked out of the Alaska governor’s mansion for more than 20 years, but this year’s highly competitive race could break that streak.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, is up against Republican Bernadette Wilson and two others in the Last Frontier’s four-way, ranked-choice general election. Democrat Tom Begich advanced from the primary, but dropped out and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, helping to clear a path.

If elected, 37-year-old Kreiss-Tomkins would become the youngest governor in Alaska’s history and the first Democrat to win the seat since 1998. Independent Bill Walker served a term as governor in 2014.

Cook Political Report rates the race as lean Democratic, after shifting it out of the toss-up column earlier this month. Alaska is also host to a highly competitive Senate race, but the election handicapper cited GOP sources in the state as being “more worried” about losing the governor’s mansion.

DDHQ’s forecast gives Kreiss-Tomkins a 62 percent probability of a win.

The race to replace term-limited Gov. Brian Kemp (R) in Georgia is deadlocked between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson.

The latest Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll found Jackson at 46 percent and Bottoms at 45 percent, a statistical dead heat.

If Bottoms can break through, she could become the Peach State’s first Black governor and first woman governor – and end the GOP’s two-decade winning streak for the office.

But Jackson, a billionaire, has the clear fundraising advantage as Election Day nears, and has spent more than $108 million of his own money on the race.

Politico reported on Tuesday that Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) was sending $1 million to boost Bottoms’ bid.

Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up. DDHQ gives it the same rating, with Bottoms narrowly favored at a 54 percent probability, after Jackson gained some ground in recent weeks.

Talarico, Paxton in dead heat for Texas Senate, Abbott leads governor’s race: Poll

Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are in a dead heat for the Senate in Texas, according to new polling of one of the cycle’s most closely watched contests.

Talarico notched 48 percent to Paxton’s 46 percent in new numbers from Emerson College Polling and The Hill, a result within the poll’s margin of error. Another 5 percent were undecided, and 1 percent picked Libertarian Ted Brown.

When undecided voters were asked which candidate they lean toward, Talarico’s support jumped to 49 percent, Paxton to 48 percent and Brown to 3 percent.

“Since August, Talarico’s support has slowly inched up by about a point each month, from 46% to 48%, while Paxton has hovered between 46% and 47%,” said Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling.

Meanwhile, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) boasted a slight lead in the Emerson polling of the gubernatorial race as he tries for a fourth term.

Abbott scored 49 percent to Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s 45 percent, while Libertarian Pat Dixon snagged 1 percent and another 4 percent were undecided.

When undecided voters were forced to a choice, Abbott jumped to 51 percent, Hinojosa to 47 percent and Dixon to 2 percent.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) rates the Texas Senate a toss-up, with Talarico narrowly favored. The governor’s race has a “lean Republican” rating, a step short of being a toss-up.

The Emerson College Polling Texas survey was conducted Oct. 17-19 among 1,000 likely Texas voters and has a credibility interval, similar to a poll’s margin of error, of plus or minus 3.1 percent.

articles.title: Don’t let Elissa Slotkin scare new grads out of public service
articles.summary: One can only wonder why Slotkin deems it a good idea to break from the bipartisan path and discourage capable young graduates from staffing the government.
articles.body:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) is warning young job-seekers not to seek a position with the Trump administration, lest they harm their careers.

As she put it: “I want young people coming out of school to say, should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity. I want them to be like, Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that,” she said at a University of Chicago forum last week. “I want that deterrence message.”

To be sure, some federal agencies have been especially politicized — think here of working for ICE or perhaps even the Department of Justice legal team going after Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.). But far more current federal job openings are for positions that provide the nuts and bolts of government on which Americans rely. They carry no political valence.

That is the conclusion one must draw from the “early careers: recent graduates ” section of the USAJobs site operated by the federal Office of Personnel Management.

One wonders whether Slotkin would object to a new grad taking a job as staff psychologist for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (starting pay $107,000 in Denton, Texas), or as a cybersecurity specialist for the Defense Information Systems Agency ($57,000, Fort Meade, Md.,). What about an industrial hygienist for the Occupational Safety and Health Administration ($50,000, Overland Park, Kan.)? Or a safety engineer at the Federal Aviation Administration ($53,000)?

These cannot simply be dismissed as political positions. Many are permanent jobs not subject to presidential whim. They represent the sinews of public service, the “human resources” that allow us to be confident in our food supply, air traffic, workplace safety and much more. These services rely on young people stepping into positions being rapidly vacated by retirees.

As the Federal News Network has reported, “105,858 retired from federal service in 2025. The Defense Department saw the largest number of employees leave via retirement at 31,689, while the departments of Veterans Affairs, Homeland Security, Agriculture, Justice, Treasury and Health and Human Services all saw more than 6,000 employees leave via retirement.”

Slotkin’s discouraging words come on top of a worrisome trend: Graduates of the nation’s leading professional schools of government have been choosing private or non-profit employment instead of public service. In a survey of 13 such schools, including Harvard, Berkeley and Princeton, just a third of graduates chose to work for government. Even that may overstate the trend; their student bodies have included many non-U.S. students who return to their own countries.

One can argue that our core political debate centers on the size and scope of government. But that is a debate about relatively modest adjustments — about the extent of the welfare state, for instance, not about whether we should have a safety net. It is about how the IRS should discourage tax cheats, not whether it should do so.

Our student loan system has reflected the need for new graduates to choose to work for government. The Public Service Student Loan program forgives the balance of such a loan if the borrower has made 120 monthly payments. One might dispute whether government (or non-profit) employment is really more valuable than work in the private sector, but both parties have voted for the loan forgiveness law, which began in 2007 during the George W. Bush administration, was preserved by the Obama administration and survived the changes of last year’s “big beautiful” tax bill.

One can only wonder why Slotkin deems it a good idea to break from the bipartisan path and discourage capable young graduates from staffing the government.

Howard Husock is a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and author of “The Projects: A New History of Public Housing.”
