articles.title: Social Security says it’s ‘corrected’ tens of millions of records. Here’s why
articles.summary: The agency said it has added 17 million death dates to records that previously had none and updated citizenship information.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The Social Security Administration says it has “corrected” nearly 15% of active Social Security numbers since the start of the Trump administration as part of an ongoing effort to improve the accuracy and integrity of its database.

The agency said Tuesday it has added 17 million death dates to records that previously had none and updated citizenship information in roughly 25 million records where it was missing.

“This is the first time SSA has undertaken an effort of this scale, and I am proud of the work we have done to strengthen the foundation of identity data relied upon throughout government and the economy,” SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a release.

SSA said it is still correcting an additional 8 1/2 million records with “inaccurate citizenship status.” The agency said it has also implemented “stronger internal controls” to prevent future data entry errors.

The database cleanup is the most comprehensive in the agency’s 91-year history, SSA said, and underscores a government-wide commitment to “safeguarding identity data” and “preventing fraud.”

Tuesday’s announcement did not say how many, if any, of the corrected records were tied to improper payments or suspected fraud. NewsNation asked SSA for that number by email, but the agency did not respond.

SSA did not provide an estimate of how much the database cleanup could save taxpayers.

Were millions of dead people getting Social Security checks?

Social Security’s database drew headlines last year after President Trump and Elon Musk erroneously implied that millions of dead people were receiving benefits, vastly overstating the scale of the problem.

The claims were based on SSA records for millions of people born more than a century ago who had no death date on file.

Then-acting Social Security Commissioner Lee Dudek later clarified that a missing death date didn’t mean that benefits were still being paid.

A 2023 inspector general report found that Social Security had no death information on file for about 18.9 million people born in 1920 or earlier but noted that “almost none” were receiving payments.

At the time, SSA officials said updating the death information would have “limited or no benefit” to its programs and estimated the effort would cost $5.5 million to $9.7 million.

Still, the inspector general recommended that SSA add death information to the records, cautioning that those Social Security numbers could allow for a “wide range of potential abuse.”

Federal data show about 92,000 retired workers aged 99 or older received Social Security benefits in June 2026, a number that has hardly changed in recent years and is comparable to the size of the U.S. centenarian population .

Noncitizens who are in the U.S. legally can receive Social Security retirement benefits if they meet the program’s eligibility requirements, but those in the country illegally don’t qualify.

Improper retirement payments do happen, but they’re relatively rare.

SSA’s 2025 report found that 99.91% of Old-Age and Survivors Insurance payments were free of overpayments and 99.96% were free of underpayments. It estimated $1.62 billion in improper payments out of roughly $1.29 trillion in OASI benefit payments.

articles.title: Acton responds to Ramaswamy’s ad: ‘It’s despicable’
articles.summary: Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee in Ohio’s governor race, responded for the first time to a controversial campaign ad from her opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, that featured her estranged mother calling her a liar. “A sad thing, and I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do. My mother is not well,” Acton told CBS…
articles.body:
Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee in Ohio’s governor race, responded for the first time to a controversial campaign ad from her opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, that featured her estranged mother calling her a liar.

“A sad thing, and I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do. My mother is not well,” Acton told CBS affiliate WBNS . “So, I think it’s despicable.”

In another interview with CNN , Acton noted how “many people are outraged by this because so many people have experienced some sort of trauma or abuse in their lives.”

“And so I‘m much more focused on a message that reaches them than on the antics of an out-of-touch billionaire who would be a danger to my state,” she continued.

Acton has talked about experiencing physical and sexual abuse, along with neglect, during her childhood. Her mother stayed with her stepfather even after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old, according to court documents . Acton says the last time she saw her mother was in court the day her stepfather was taken into custody.

Acton alleged the attack ad was part of a “ lifelong pattern ” for Ramaswamy, pointing to personal attacks he levied toward Nikki Haley’s daughter during a GOP debate in the 2016 presidential election.

Ramaswamy confirmed Tuesday that his campaign funded the ad, which showed Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her a “liar” and insinuating she suffered from mental health issues. When asked by a local outlet if he stood by the claims in the ad, Ramaswamy stated, “To be clear, this is not new.”

“Her mother has spoken out for years, and I don’t know Amy Acton’s mother and I’ve never met Amy Acton either. What I do know is that Amy Acton has been repeatedly and serially dishonest during this campaign,” Ramaswamy said.

In a statement to The Associated Press, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy’s campaign said Acton’s mother was not paid for the ad, adding that it will air online and on TV as Election Day draws near.

His campaign is also reportedly spending $4 million to air the spot statewide, first reported by Axios , doubling down despite criticism from both sides of the aisle .

Acton’s brother condemned the ad, saying in a statement to CBS News it was a “desperate” dig from Ramaswamy in a tight gubernatorial race and that their mother “stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”

articles.title: White House threatens Politico with 'consequences' if it doesn't retract Susie Wiles reporting
articles.summary: White House counsel William Scharf gave Politico 48 hours to retract its reporting claiming President Donald Trump was mulling replacing chief of staff Susie Wiles.
articles.body: Politico has issued a correction and re-examined multiple articles after the White House threatened "consequences" if the outlet doesn't retract its recent reporting on President Donald Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles, Fox News Digital has confirmed. In a letter addressed to Politico's global editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger on Monday, White House counsel William Scharf slammed three "demonstrably false and defamatory articles" about Wiles, including claims that Trump was mulling Wiles' ouster, and that he had a "freak-out" when Politico published its story. "These publications reflect far more than sloppy reporting or an unfortunate, inadvertent reliance on unreliable sources. They instead reveal a disturbing pattern of the publication of sensational falsehoods despite direct, on-the-record refutations from senior White House officials and even the President of the United States himself, as well as documentary evidence provided to Politico, all of which established clearly that claims central to Politico's planned reporting were false. Put simply, your publication was told the truth and presented with corroborating evidence, and yet chose to publish fanciful fiction regardless," Scharf wrote in the letter first reported by Axios that has been obtained by Fox News Digital. WHITE HOUSE CONFIRMS APPEAL AS TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE EXTENDS RULING RESTORING CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO ACCESS "This is not a question of competing interpretations, editorial judgment, or political disagreement. It is a question of whether a major news organization may knowingly publish demonstrably false factual allegations, disregard documentary evidence contradicting those allegations, and then hide behind anonymous sources when confronted with the truth. It may not. I therefore demand that Politico retract these defamatory articles and issue corrections promptly, or face the consequences," he later continued. Scharf gave Politico "48 hours" to reverse its reporting and issue an apology to both Trump and Wiles before the White House explores "appropriate and available legal remedies." WHITE HOUSE REPORTERS REACT TO KATIE ZACHARIA'S 'BRUTAL' EXIT AS TRUMP'S PRESS SECRETARY "The White House has no obligation to pretend that this persistent conduct is consistent with responsible journalism. Nor should Politico expect that its institutional behavior will be insulated from scrutiny. After all, freedom of the press is not a professional exemption from accountability," Scharf told Greenberg. "I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives. Failure to do so or otherwise respond justifying Politico's publications within 48 hours will prompt an immediate review of Politico's relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies." Politico responded on Wednesday, insisting it strives for accuracy in its reporting and "categorically rejects the false accusations" that it "chose to publish fanciful fiction" and "purposeful falsehoods designed to mislead the public." "That said, Politico takes seriously assertions like those made in your letter. Accordingly, consistent with its commitment to ensuring its reporting is as accurate as possible, Politico re-examined all three articles identified in your letter and did follow up reporting," Politico's attorney wrote in a letter obtained by Fox News Digital. "As a result, Politico determined it was appropriate to correct one of the three articles identified in your letter," the letter continued. Politico did not offer an apology to Trump and Wiles or correct the report that Trump was considering moving on from Wiles. Instead, Politico corrected an article to note that Wiles simply offered "positive reinforcement" for then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia's Fox News appearance on "Hannity" last week before she stepped down, but did not play a direct role in booking the interview. BIDEN-ERA FBI RECORDS REVEAL SPRAWLING WILES MONITORING AS BURIED CONTACTS SURFACE "The updated version of that article, reflecting the information obtained through Politico's further reporting, has now been published. Promptly and transparently making corrections, as Politico has done here, is a hallmark of journalistic ethics and integrity, and of the very professionalism your letter falsely claims Politico is lacking," Politico's attorney wrote. Politico has been in the crosshairs of the Trump administration in recent weeks as among the outlets that were banned by the White House last month, which had been reversed by a judge's ruling. "To be clear, any error that you could identify in Politico's reporting about the President or his administration would not excuse the White House's unconstitutional retaliation and discrimination against Politico for the content of its news coverage," Politico's response said. "The White House's efforts to retaliate against Politico for its constitutionally protected journalism, and to discriminate against Politico based on what the President perceives to be its editorial viewpoint is a profound affront to the most fundamental constitutional rights," the response continued. "Politico will defend its journalism and the right of its reporters to pursue their mission and report fearlessly on the President and other White House officials for the benefit of the American public, notwithstanding the White House's ongoing attempts to intimidate Politico and chill and punish that reporting." When reached for comment, the White House suggested Politico has not done enough and "should be embarrassed." "Politico should apologize to its dwindling readership for knowingly publishing lies. Its reporters and editors were presented with irrefutable evidence disproving their previous reporting and current allegations, yet chose to ignore facts, peddle lies, and manufacture controversy," White House spokesperson Danielle Alvarez told Fox News Digital. "The facts are indisputable: the Chief of Staff had absolutely nothing to do with booking or authorizing any interview. Politicoâs reckless disregard for the truth is a disgrace to journalism," the spokesperson continued. "At this point, the question isnât whether Politico got the facts wrong â itâs why its editors continue to publish claims they know are false. Politico should be embarrassed." articles.title: Russia and Iran are making copycats of China’s Great Firewall
articles.summary: The repressive leaders of Iran and Russia seek to carve their people off from the global internet to maintain their hold on power.
articles.body:
For almost three months, the vast majority of people in Iran were cut off from the internet . Iranian authorities initiated a nationwide internet blackout in February as the U.S. and Israel launched military strikes against the country. With bombs falling from the sky, Iranians could not contact their loved ones, access information about danger zones or look up potentially lifesaving medical guidance.

The blackout — the longest of its kind in the world — marked Iran as one of the world’s worst environments for internet freedom, according to our new edition of Freedom House’s annual Freedom on the Net index, released today.

Iran’s internet blackout was accompanied by a host of other repressive measures, the culmination of an effort to restructure the Iranian internet to isolate the Iranian people. A similar effort is underway in Russia, pursued by Vladimir Putin and his cronies.

Authorities in both countries seek to limit their people to a domestic internet run by government-aligned services, on which the government maintains a stranglehold on information and crushes dissenting speech. The world’s democracies should ensure this effort fails, so that the people of Iran and Russia have a means to challenge their leaders’ authoritarian grasp on power.

Officials in Iran and Russia have pursued an effort to restrict access to global internet services and push people to government-aligned alternatives in a drive to replicate China’s extensive censorship system, known as the Great Firewall . Whereas the Great Firewall was built into China’s infrastructure from the ground up, the governments of Russia and Iran must reengineer their systems to facilitate systemic censorship and coerce their people to comply.

State-backed services are favored for their compliance with government demands for censorship and surveillance, enabling repressive leaders to maintain control on information and political power.

Over the past year, Russian authorities escalated restrictions on Meta’s WhatsApp and the home-grown messaging platform Telegram, slowing speeds drastically. Russian officials have pushed the adoption of Max — a messaging platform developed by government-friendly company VKontakte, or VK — and loaded with surveillance features.

For all their failings, global social media platforms allow for connection and exchange beyond a country’s borders and offer a venue to challenge censorship orders.

Both governments have also restricted access to commercial virtual private networks, or VPNs, which protect internet traffic and enable people to sidestep website censorship.

Iranian officials criminalized the use of VPNs deemed “unauthorized” in 2024, pushing people to use state-licensed providers that allow authorities to carry out censorship and surveillance with ease. During the ongoing conflict, the price of state-backed VPNs skyrocketed, as did the costs on the black market — one person reported paying around $20 for one gigabyte of data, about one-fifth of the average monthly wage.

Iranian and Russian authorities have wielded the pain of internet shutdowns to drive people toward the authoritarian-aligned internet stack. Russian officials announced a “register of socially significant services” in September 2025, which functions as a whitelist of websites that internet providers to which must maintain access during shutdowns. The list features state media outlets and Max, as well as other state-aligned platforms like VK.

The costs of digital isolation are steep and borne by ordinary people. These efforts cut families off from their loved ones abroad, disrupt businesses and international commerce and subject people to mass censorship and surveillance. For officials in Iran and Russia, the prospect of long-term political control is worth the suffering inflicted on their people.

Democracies should work to undermine this effort, particularly by investing in technology that allows people to sidestep these methods of control. Satellite internet services can help people counter internet shutdowns, to the extent that Iranian authorities placed penalties of up to two years imprisonment for the use of unlicensed satellite services in October.

Innovation in direct-to-cell capability may make it possible to solve some of the physical limitations of satellite hubs Other tools like decentralized mesh networks and VPN-like circumvention technology play an important role as well.

In the United States, the Open Technology Fund is a model of American innovation and global leadership in technical efforts to support the open internet.

A nonprofit supported by the government since 2011 that presently operates within the U.S. Agency for Global Media, the fund supports the ecosystem of open-source anti-censorship tools, many of which are purpose-built to support people in closed countries like Iran, Russia and China. The U.S. government should expand its investment in the Open Technology Fund to ensure it has sufficient resources to continue this important work.

The repressive leaders of Iran and Russia seek to carve their people off from the global internet to maintain their hold on power. Ensuring the people can remain connected is essential to breaking that grasp.

Kian Vesteinsson is deputy director for research at Freedom House and the author of “Freedom on the Net 2026: Seismic Shifts on the Global Internet.”

articles.title: Four immigration enforcement measures we can all agree on — even under Trump
articles.summary: Opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies should not be opposing every enforcement initiative the administration establishes.
articles.body:
The news media has provided extensive, national coverage on polarizing immigration enforcement measures taking place under the Trump administration, such as border apprehensions and the escalation of ICE activities in the interior of the country. But it hasn’t provided much coverage of enforcement measures that might have bipartisan support. Here are four that should be celebrated — on both sides of the aisle.

Joint Task Force Alpha: Transnational human smuggling networks “not only seek to profit from the exploitation of migrants, but also routinely expose them to violence, injury, and even death,” according to the Office of the Attorney General. Between October 2020 and June 2021, the Department of Homeland Security rescued more than 4,000 migrants who had been abandoned by smugglers along the southwest border. And it found 250 migrants in 2020 who had died during their journey to the U.S.

On June 7, 2021, the Biden administration announced the establishment of Joint Task Force Alpha, which would use the investigative and prosecutorial resources of the Justice Department and Homeland Security to investigate and prosecute the “human smuggling and trafficking networks that exploit and endanger migrants to the United States from the Northern Triangle countries of El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and from Mexico.”

The current administration has continued the Biden administration’s task force, and expanded it along maritime borders and the northern border with Canada.

Since its creation in 2021, task force activities have resulted in more than 483 arrests, more than 436 convictions, and “substantial” forfeitures.

Unaccompanied alien children: Most unaccompanied alien children who are apprehended at the border are transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which takes care of them until they can be placed with sponsors.

More than 479,000 children were referred to the Refugee Resettlement office during the Biden administration. When the office became overwhelmed by having to process so many unaccompanied minors, it relaxed sponsor vetting .

A Health and Human Services inspector general report on a sample of children released in early 2021 found problems with sponsor screening and follow-up procedures. In 16 percent of the cases, it says, one or more sponsor safety checks “lacked any documentation indicating that the checks were conducted.”

Among children released to sponsors with pending FBI fingerprint or state child abuse registry checks, 19 percent had files that were never updated with the results. Sponsor identification documents had legibility problems in 35 percent of the cases, and the Office of Refugee Resettlement failed to conduct timely safety and well-being follow-up calls in 22 percent of the cases.

The Trump administration has tried to locate these missing children, and has prioritized the prosecution of individuals who have submitted fraudulent sponsorship applications.

Exploiting foreign agricultural workers: In a press release issued Sept. 15, the Justice Department announced an indictment charging five defendants with engaging in a scheme to defraud the H-2A visa program. This program helps farmers to fill temporary or seasonal jobs when there is a shortage of domestic workers.

The indictment alleges further that the defendants did not comply with H-2A requirements and that they demanded payments before the workers could apply for H-2A visas or begin employment. And it alleges that they prevented the agricultural workers from leaving their jobs in the United States by confiscating their passports and threatening them with violence.

U.S. Attorney Margaret E. “Meg” Heap for the Southern District of Georgia said, “We will continue to partner with our federal, state and local agencies to protect these workers, safeguard the integrity of the H-2A program and prosecute those who turn a lawful employment program into a vehicle for profit and abuse.”

Homeland Security task forces: In his executive order titled “ Protecting the American People Against Invasion ,” President Trump directed the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to establish Homeland Security task forces in all states nationwide. The order directs the attorney general, the Homeland Security secretary, and state and local law enforcement agencies to work together “to end the presence of criminal cartels, foreign gangs, and transnational criminal organizations throughout the United States.”

To date, there are 59 task force offices, with more than 9,000 personnel and 440 state and local law agency partners.

Opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies should not be opposing every enforcement initiative the administration establishes. Prosecuting human smugglers and violent criminal organizations, protecting unaccompanied alien children, and preventing foreign workers from being exploited are objectives that should have bipartisan support.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years.

articles.title: Judge blocks most DHS field operations focused on voter fraud
articles.summary: A federal judge in California blocked most Department of Homeland Security (DHS) field operations focused on voter fraud in a Wednesday court ruling. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, appointed under former President Biden, barred the DHS from conducting “elections-related field operations and field interviews” in nine states — California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York,…
articles.body:
A federal judge in California blocked most Department of Homeland Security (DHS) field operations focused on voter fraud in a Wednesday court ruling.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, appointed under former President Biden, barred the DHS from conducting “elections-related field operations and field interviews” in nine states — California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Operations are only blocked if the DHS or Secretary Markwayne Mullin suspects people who they “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.”

“Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in her 19-page ruling . “Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote.”

Martínez-Olguín continued that the relevant operations this lawsuit concerned were reliant on “a target list of such individuals from a variety of sources” which were “voluminous and unreliable.”

She noted that “even under the best conditions, there is a high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents.”

“The time limitations implemented during the Surge further exacerbate the risk of error,” Martínez-Olguín said, adding that DHS agents were ordered to take “no more than twelve minutes to eliminate a person from the target list using the commercial databases.”

The ruling comes less than two weeks from the midterm election on Nov. 3, as Mullin has attempted to launch operations across the country into alleged voter fraud. Martínez-Olguín’s orders will remain in effect until Election Day at 8 p.m. “or when polling places close.”

This also deals a blow to the Trump administration’s effort to monitor polling places and combat alleged voter fraud. Other lawsuits filed against the administration are pending, including one where the city of Denver argued ICE agents violated federal law that prohibited the presence of “ troops at polls .”

Mullin said earlier this year that ICE would “only” be deployed at polls during the midterms if a “threat” arises.

The Trump administration is still pursuing restrictions on mail-in voting and creating voter lists — though the window to implement these rules is closing.

When asked about the ruling, a DHS spokesperson told The Hill the department was “laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders.”

“We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson continued.

articles.title: Talarico challenges ‘Low T’ Paxton to debate
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico challenged his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), to a debate hosted by TMZ, renewing his calls for the Republican to face him ahead of the November election. In an interview with TMZ, Talarico said Paxton has repeatedly ignored his invitations to debate him and suggested the entertainment…
articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico challenged his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), to a debate hosted by TMZ, renewing his calls for the Republican to face him ahead of the November election.

In an interview with TMZ, Talarico said Paxton has repeatedly ignored his invitations to debate him and suggested the entertainment news outlet host a debate between the two after learning one of its reporters had recently pressed Paxton about his reluctance to debate.

“Ken Paxton has refused to debate and that’s pretty low-T behavior in my book,” Talarico said, referencing Paxton’s “Low-T Talarico” insult on his masculinity in an attack ad.

Paxton on Wednesday told a TMZ reporter he would be open to a debate but didn’t “want to end up with the CNN reporter covering the debate.”

“Maybe TMZ should host this debate,” Talarico said, saying the outlet can “get a hold of Ken Paxton easier than most journalists do.”

Talarico pushed back on Paxton’s conditions for the debate, telling TMZ that he had also extended the offer to host the debate on more conservative-leaning outlets such as Fox News.

Paxton has not agreed to debate Talarico, despite the repeated public challenges from his Democratic opponent.

The latest exchange comes as the two candidates face off in a competitive race for the Senate seat held by Sen. John Cornyn (R), whom Paxton defeated in a primary runoff earlier this year with an endorsement from President Trump.

Trump has placed the blame on Cornyn and other Republicans for making the general election seemingly more difficult for the state attorney general in the deep-red state.

Cornyn warned that Paxton’s several scandals could be an issue for Republicans, saying the attorney general “endangers the seat as the nominee.”

Trump stood by his endorsee, calling out Cornyn and conservative strategist Karl Rove for not doing enough to support Paxton.

“John Cornyn, and his Liddle’ Buddy, Super RINO, Karl Rove, are doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton, the Greatest Attorney General in the History of Texas, and one of the Best in the United States, to win the upcoming Midterm Election against a Radical Left Lunatic,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

articles.body:
Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) on Wednesday said he and his family are safe in the wake of an assassination threat from a 17-year-old.

“I am grateful to the FBI and law enforcement for stopping this threat. My family and I are safe, and I remain focused on serving the people of Texas’ 3rd District,” Self said Wednesday on the social platform X .

“Preserving our constitutional republic from radical Islam means accepting the costs that come with it—name-calling, threats, and worse,” he added. “Our Founders believed this country was worth the sacrifice. I served 25 years in the military because defending freedom was worth the sacrifice. This only strengthens my resolve. I will not back down.”

Local outlet WFAA reported Wednesday that a 17-year-old was arrested and charged by the FBI for an assassination plot against Self meant for an event over the weekend. Investigators told the outlet the boy had also plotted to undertake a North Texas-based terrorist attack for ISIS.

The 17-year-old was arrested earlier this month in the wake of obtaining a firearm, federal law enforcement sources said, per WFAA. The federal government had custody of the boy, whose name is not public, the outlet reported.

The reported threat against Self follows notable instances of political violence in recent years, including assassination attempts against President Trump and the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

articles.title: Has Congress traded our kids for Big Tech?
articles.summary: Our government, rather than acting appropriately, continues to cozy up to Big Tech.
articles.body:
Five years ago, Frances Haugen sat before a Senate subcommittee and delivered a warning Congress could hardly misunderstand.

“Congressional action is needed,” the former Facebook employee testified on Oct. 5, 2021. “They won’t solve this crisis without your help.”

Five years later, the Kids Online Safety Act , which has wide bipartisan support, still has not become law. How many more hearings does Congress need before its concern becomes a binding obligation to protect children?

I recently sat down with Haugen for a conversation at a pre-release screening of “The Social Reckoning,” a new film about how Meta and social media platforms have manipulated and influenced us. I asked her what most parents are wondering: What continues to prevent Congress from turning bipartisan support for children’s online safety into law? Her answer focused on the money at stake and the financial incentives Big Tech has to preserve the status quo.

That conversation brought me back to the question Washington has left unanswered. When lawmakers acknowledge the dangers of social media for children but fail to enact any protections, whose interests does the delay serve?

Haugen’s whistleblower testimony against Meta was never simply that she criticized Facebook. She brought internal documents into public view and told Congress that the company repeatedly resolved conflicts between profitability and safety in favor of profit. These were allegations supported by an insider’s disclosures, which have demanded investigation, transparency and accountability.

“They [Meta] fear the blowback more than they fear the harm,” Haugen told me.

These statements should cause everyone to question why our elected leaders haven’t taken meaningful action. These companies put a higher value on profitability than a duty of care to protect children online. Our government, rather than acting appropriately, continues to cozy up to Big Tech on the promise of data centers and AI development, all the while ignoring the outcry for change.

Technology companies have lobbied with over $50 million against bills aimed at basic protection and care for our children, thus sending us the message that our kids’ worth falls below the value of protecting technology companies.

Congress cannot plausibly claim it never received the warning. Nor can it claim that lawmakers have been unable to find common ground. Sens. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) first introduced the Kids Online Safety Act in February 2022. On July 30, 2024, the Senate approved a package combining the act with children’s privacy legislation by a vote of 91-3. That package never became law.

The history since then matters. We should be precise about it.

The House passed a different package, the Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act , on June 29, by a margin of 267-117. While it contains safeguards worth discussing, its provision addressing harms to minors expressly says it must not be construed to impose a duty of care on covered platforms. That is a consequential departure from the Senate approach.

On Aug. 5, the Senate Commerce Committee advanced the Kids Online Safety Act again . On Sept. 30, Blumenthal sought its passage by unanimous consent. Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) objected , citing concerns about constitutionally protected speech, and the attempt failed.

Freedom of speech is a right afforded to all Americans, and I strongly support it. However, I and other child safety advocates disagree with Paul. This isn’t an issue of free speech; it is an issue of conduct. These companies are not only knowingly engaging in practices that cause harm to our children online, but also are profiting from them and amplifying them, all while cowering behind the Communications Decency Act’s Section 230 shield . Congress has taken steps, but it has failed to finish the job.

As president of the National Center on Sexual Exploitation, and as a father raising teenagers, I see the burden this failure places on families. The harm has been well documented by whistleblowers like Haugen with internal documents from behind the closed doors of one of the most powerful companies in the world. We simply cannot put the responsibility on parents and families alone; we need action and it’s long overdue.

Congress should enact a carefully drawn, enforceable duty of care focused on platform design, supported by strong privacy defaults, accessible safeguards and independent scrutiny. Companies should have to demonstrate what they are doing to prevent and mitigate foreseeable harms within the law’s scope.

This story asks whether Congress has traded our kids for Big Tech. It is a demand for accountability, not an allegation that every opponent has been bought. Lawmakers can disagree sincerely. They must still explain how their proposed path will protect children — and when it will become law.

Voters should ask every U.S. representative and senator: What enforceable protections will you support? What changes do you require? When will you vote?

Haugen took a personal risk to bring Congress information it needed to act. Families have spent years pressing lawmakers to use it.

Our children are growing up while Washington negotiates. They cannot get those years back.

Richie Hamm is president of the National Center on Sexual Exploitation, a national non-profit organization exposing the links between all forms of sexual exploitation such as child sexual abuse, prostitution, sex trafficking and the public health harms of pornography.

articles.title: High-ranking Virginia state Democrat charged in public corruption case
articles.summary: Virginia State Senator L. Louise Lucas charged in public corruption case, DOJ says
articles.body: NORFOLK, Va. — Federal authorities on Thursday charged a prominent Virginia Democrat with racketeering and a money laundering conspiracy as part of an alleged public corruption case involving a cannabis business she co-owns. Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a frequent critic of President Donald Trump who is one of the most powerful Democrats in the state, surrendered to authorities Thursday. She was also charged with conspiracy to distribute marijuana. A half dozen others, including Lucas’ daughters, were also in custody and charged in the alleged scheme. The investigation into the 82-year-old Lucas predates the Trump administration, NBC News previously reported. But the Justice Department’s move, just 12 days before a midterm election, is unusual, as federal authorities have typically avoided taking overt investigative steps against political figures so close to an election. Lucas is not up for re-election this year but has ties to prominent Democrats who are on the ballot. Lucas said in a statement on social media that she will not be intimidated, or back down. “Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother,” Lucas wrote. “I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back and I’m not stopping now.” Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to in Norfolk, Virginia for a press conference announcing the charges. Blanche said that Lucas, who has been a public servant for years, put her own financial interests above the people she was elected to serve. “The Department of Justice intends to prove that Senator Lucas violated the trust of the people of Portsmouth and Chesapeake, Virginia, and of her state senate colleagues,” he said. “Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself.” The Justice Department has brought several controversial cases against Trump’s political targets in his second term. Three weeks before the midterms, federal officials searched the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Ohmar of Minnesota in an immigration-related investigation and seized her phone. She has said she will not be silenced. The Justice Department has typically not brought political cases within 60 days of an election, but the Blanche on Thursday dismissed those concerns. “It’s not even a rule, it’s a practice,” he said. He noted Lucas wasn’t up for reelection. “The justice manual speaks very clearly about what the Department of Justice can and can’t do, and we cannot bring a charge if our purpose is improper,” Blanche said. But he said the case was correctly brought. In May, federal agents searched Lucas’ office in Portsmouth, along with a business she co-owns called The Cannabis Outlet, which is located on High Street. U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., said his communications with Lucas were monitored and that the Justice Department had become Trump’s “own personal law firm, with his former personal attorney carrying out vendettas on Trump’s political enemies.” A reporter with WAVY, an NBC affiliate, also received a notification letter showing that his communications with Lucas’ number had been swept up in the wire. The indictment alleges that members of the conspiracy “used various business entities” to “disguise the proceeds of illegal marijuana distribution,” and that Lucas “used her political position in the Virginia state senate to insulate” the enterprise “from criminal scrutiny, to further the goal of wealth accumulation.” In one intercepted phone call in February 2026 with an alleged co-conspirator who has not been indicted, Lucas allegedly said that this was their “last chance at generational wealth,” adding “I’ve gotten too old to not be greedy.” Lucas has been a proponent of marijuana legalization in Virginia. The state now allows for possession of marijuana for adults over 21, but recreational marijuana sales remain unlawful. That is set to change; this summer, the governor and state legislators announced an agreement to allow the licensed retail sale of marijuana beginning July 1, 2027. Lucas’ political career began more than four decades ago, when she was elected to the Portsmouth City Council. She was elected to the Virginia General Assembly in 1991. The Virginia Senate consists of 40 members who serve four year terms and receive an annual salary of $18,000, a figure set in 1988. Members also receive mileage reimbursement and a per diem during the General Assembly session. U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, the former judge and Fox News host Trump named as the top federal prosecutor in the nation’s capital, attempted and failed to indict six sitting members of Congress over a social media video that Trump disliked. A criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey over an Instagram photo of seashells remains ongoing.

articles.title: Politico corrects story on Susie Wiles after White House threatens ‘consequences’
articles.summary: Politico issued a correction late Wednesday to a story it published about White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and the backstory on what led to ousted press secretary Katie Zacharia’s firing last week. The outlet originally reported that Wiles helped set up interviews for Zacharia on Fox News, a widely panned series of media…
articles.body:
Politico issued a correction late Wednesday to a story it published about White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and the backstory on what led to ousted press secretary Katie Zacharia’s firing last week.

The outlet originally reported that Wiles helped set up interviews for Zacharia on Fox News, a widely panned series of media hits that ultimately ended with the press secretary’s firing last week.

“An earlier version of this report, including its headline, mischaracterized the role White House chief of staff Susie Wiles played in then-press secretary Katie Zacharia’s interview with Sean Hannity on Fox News,” the outlet wrote in its correction . “POLITICO’s follow-up reporting indicates she did not play a direct role in setting up the interview.”

The correction came after the White House sent a letter to the outlet demanding it correct the record on Wiles’s role in Zacharia’s hits on Fox News, Axios reported , with the West Wing saying the outlet could face unspecified consequences over the inaccurate report.

Fox News also refuted Politico’s reporting, the outlet noted.

This week’s episode between the White House and Politico comes amid a broader period of tensions between President Trump’s administration and the press corps.

The outlet was one of three Trump sought to ban from working from the White House, and the West Wing has banned the political news outlet from Air Force One on at least one occasion since.

The story in Politico is just the latest in a string of reports that have popped up suggesting Trump was losing faith in Wiles .

Trump and his aides have seemingly grown more frustrated with the media in recent days, with the president snapping at reporters while answering questions and reportedly floating the idea of moving the press corps from the White House to another location.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) slammed special envoy Steve Witkoff’s characterization of Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian,” instead calling the Russian leader “an evil killer.”

Cramer also declared he would rather die in a Russian prison than have someone praise Putin as a “humanitarian” to earn his release.

“Humanitarian wouldn’t be one of the first ten million words I’d think of to describe Vladimir Putin. He is anything but a humanitarian,” Cramer said when asked about Witkoff’s comments, which came in connection with the release of an American who had been held in a Russian prison.

Cramer noted Witkoff has a “different job” as a diplomat than he does as a senator, but the North Dakota senator minced no words in denouncing Putin, calling him “as bad as it gets.”

“Obviously the release of an American is a big deal,” he acknowledged.

“All I can say is if I’m ever captured by Vladimir Putin, I’d rather die in a prison in Russia than have somebody on my behalf refer to Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian,” he declared.

“That said, I don’t plan to go to Russia anytime soon,” he added.

Witkoff, President Trump’s top diplomatic negotiator, praised Putin as a “humanitarian” after the Russian leader announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American who had been incarcerated in Russia for the past four years. The United States considered him wrongfully detained.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff told Putin last week at a meeting in St. Petersburg after Hubbard’s announced release. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.”

Other Republicans have also criticized Witkoff’s comments.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called it an “embarrassing and outrageous thing to say.”

“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian.’ What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis posted on the social platform X.

articles.title: Members are nervous about opening day disruptions
articles.summary: Concerns regarding potential political interference and partisan challenges have heightened ahead of the scheduled opening of the new Congress on Jan. 3.
articles.body:
The opening day of a new Congress has historically been a celebratory occasion as families and constituents of newly elected members cram the House galleries for the swearings-in. Next Jan. 3, however, is fraught as concern rises over possible disruptions.

The mob attack on the Capitol during the electoral vote count for president on Jan. 6, 2021 still haunts those who were present. Members and support staff were herded into a subterranean room for three hours of sheer terror until reinforcements arrived to relieve the overwhelmed Capitol police. Presumably, precautions are being taken this time to prevent a recurrence of comparable chaos and violence.

Yet, there is an overriding concern that President Trump’s attempts to meddle in and manipulate the midterms could cast doubt on so many elections that the House would be thrown into utter turmoil on Jan. 3.

The president’s efforts to undermine this year’s midterm elections are legion. Last Friday, the Justice Department warned California state election officials they could be exposed to federal criminal liability if they count ballots from voters that the administration has flagged as “potential noncitizens.” Previously, the administration has tried everything from convincing states to redraw their congressional district maps to placing new restrictions on mail-in voting, to deploying federal agents to polling places , and even to seizing voting machines.

Most of the heavy-handed attempts at election manipulation have been thwarted by the states or the courts. Yet the efforts were clear signals that the administration may pull out all the stops if Democrats win control of one of both houses of Congress.

The process in the House for certifying the election of members seems straightforward. On opening day, the House Clerk conducts an electronic quorum call from the names of those members-elect for whom state certifications of election have been received. After that, the Speaker is elected, then members-elect are asked to rise to be sworn-in. If a challenge to the election of any member has been received from that person’s election opponent, by statute that member is asked to stand aside and the contest is then referred to a committee for investigation.

It is also allowed, under the precedents, for any member-elect to challenge the seating of another member-elect. This was done in 2021 when Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) demanded that all members-elect from the states of Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin – 67 in all from both parties – not be sworn. House Majority Leader-elect Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) trumped Roy’s demand with a privileged resolution directing the Speaker to swear-in all members-elect. Hoyer’s resolution was adopted, 371-2 , with even Roy voting in favor.

One of the most sensational election disputes on the House floor in the last half century occurred in 1985 over a seat in the “bloody eighth” District of Indiana – the so-called McIntyre-McCloskey race . When Speaker Tip O’Neill (D-Mass.) asked members to rise to be sworn, Majority Leader-elect Jim Wright (D-Texas) rose to object to the swearing-in of Rep.-elect Rick McIntyre (R-Ind.) who had beaten incumbent Rep. Frank McCloskey (D-Ind.). McIntyre had presented the requisite certificate of election from the secretary of state of Indiana. He had won the election by a razor thin margin of 34 votes .

Wright claimed his challenge was based on “facts and statements that I consider reliable.” O’Neill was forced to direct McIntyre to remain seated. The contest was referred to a three-member task force of two Democrats and one Republican. The inquiry lasted nearly four months until Democrat McCloskey was declared the winner by four votes. Still, the unprecedented episode became a rallying-cry of outrage for Republicans. Among other things, it eventually elevated a backbench bomb-thrower named Newt Gingrich to the speakership ten years later.

Last week, two House members of opposing parties, Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.), began circulating a letter to their colleagues urging them to join in a pledge to recognize the legitimacy of those members-elect whose elections have been certified by their states. The pledge goes on to bind signers of the letter to oppose “ any attempt to refuse or delay the seating of any Member-elect .”

It is a valiant effort but will not likely garner a significant number of House signatures. Members are reluctant to commit themselves to future hypotheticals until all the facts are known. Election disputes and their resolution do have legitimacy under the law and precedents. They can, however, become extremely dangerous if used in large numbers as partisan bludgeons to stupefy the House.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran culminating as chief-of-staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” and “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

articles.title: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas charged with public corruption
articles.summary: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D) was charged and brought into custody Thursday, according to an unsealed indictment from the Department of Justice (DOJ). The DOJ alleges Lucas and her family members engaged in a racketeering conspiracy related to a family marijuana business. The indictment says Lucas obtained large quantities of illegal marijuana, sold…
articles.body:
Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D) was charged and brought into custody Thursday, according to an unsealed indictment from the Department of Justice (DOJ).

The DOJ alleges Lucas and her family members engaged in a racketeering conspiracy related to a family marijuana business. The indictment says Lucas obtained large quantities of illegal marijuana, sold it and used the proceeds from the sale to purchase more illegal marijuana. Lucas is also accused of using her political influence for her own benefit.

Lucas shared a statement to the social platform X Thursday, saying she “will not back down” against the DOJ’s charges.

“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them,” Lucas wrote. “I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”

Recreational marijuana is legal to possess in Virginia, but a legal recreational marijuana market does not begin under Virginia law until July 2027. The DOJ accused Lucas of attempting to influence the legislation for her own financial gain.

At a Thursday morning press conference, Attorney General Todd Blanche said Lucas “violated the trust” of her constituents.

“The charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” Blanche said. “Whether you are a Democrat or a Republican, an elected official or an everyday citizen, nobody is above the law.”

Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate, is a major fixture in Virginia Democratic politics. She was a major proponent of the mid-decade redistricting Virginia Democrats pushed in response to Republican efforts in other states, but the Virginia Supreme Court struck down the voter-approved map.

In May, federal authorities raided Lucas’s office in Portsmouth, Va., as well as a nearby dispensary she owned.

While Lucas is not up for election, the DOJ typically does not bring charges against political figures this close to an election. Blanche defended accusations that the indictment was for political purposes, pointing out that the investigation began in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia before President Trump returned to office.

“This is a long-running case, as alleged in the indictment,” Blanche said. “People can criticize all they want, but it was time to bring the charges. The grand jury returned an indictment, and we made the arrests.”

Lucas’s initial court appearance is scheduled for Thursday afternoon in Norfolk, Va.

Lucas, 82, has not been quiet about her support for legalized recreational marijuana, or the fact that she owns a cannabis store in Virginia.

The indictment cites some of Lucas’s “overt acts,” including a social media post from January 2022.

“I’m a 78 year grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannabis store. And I’m the last thing standing between The GOP and total control of Virginia. That’s worth an RT!” Lucas wrote.

The DOJ includes a series of checks proving payment and text messages in which members of the “Lucas Enterprise” communicate about marijuana sales. The indictment also alleges that Lucas paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for a 100 percent stake in a shell company in 2022 and expected a Virginia recreational marijuana license in return.

It is not clear how Lucas would have been able to obtain a recreational marijuana license at the time because Virginia did not pass a legal framework for commercial sales until 2026.

Blanche was asked about the discrepancy at the press conference Thursday but said he would not give information beyond what was in the indictment.

“According to the allegations in the indictment and some of the statements that were made by the co-conspirators allegedly, it ultimately is inconsistent with what the law ultimately ended up being or was at the time,” Blanche said.

articles.title: Costs, Iran voters’ top priorities for next Congress: Survey
articles.summary: A majority of respondents to a recent survey want the next Congress to focus on lowering the cost of living and winding down the Iran war. Roughly 80 percent of the 1,119 respondents to the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll said lawmakers should make lowering prices one of their highest priorities in…
articles.body:
A majority of respondents to a recent survey want the next Congress to focus on lowering the cost of living and winding down the Iran war .

Roughly 80 percent of the 1,119 respondents to the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll said lawmakers should make lowering prices one of their highest priorities in the 120th Congress.

About 70 percent of respondents also said lawmakers should prioritize ending the Iran conflict , which is approaching the eight-month mark and has resulted in the deaths of 21 U.S. service members and gas prices of more than $4 per gallon on average.

Annual inflation has risen from 2.4 percent in February to 3.7 percent last month , according to the consumer price index . Energy prices were up 20.4 percent year over year after experiencing their largest monthly jump since March, the first full month of the war.

Democrats are seeking control of Congress for the remainder of President Trump’s second term in office. Democratic lawmakers and candidates have campaigned on blocking Trump’s tariffs and forcing him to end the Iran war.

“Two years ago, Donald Trump and MAGA extremists promised that they were going to lower the high cost of living on day one. But costs haven’t gone down, costs have gone up,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said this month on the campaign trail.

Republicans, meanwhile, have argued they should remain in power to help Trump implement his agenda after former President Biden’s four years in office. The president and GOP leaders have also blasted Democrats as “communists,” after multiple left-wing candidates won primaries earlier this year.

Only about 2 in 10 respondents to the AP-NORC poll want Congress to prioritize backing Trump’s agenda, including roughly 4 in 10 Republicans — a light show of support for the president’s policies among GOP voters.

The survey, which the pollsters conducted from Oct. 8-12, has a margin of error of 3.9 percentage points.

articles.title: Generational change in Congress is coming, but it won’t fix everything
articles.summary: In less than two weeks, voters will elect what is expected to be one of the largest freshman classes of the century. It could also be one of the youngest.
articles.body:
Turnover is coming to Washington. In less than two weeks, voters will elect what is expected to be one of the largest freshman classes of the century. It could also be one of the youngest.

For the first time, more than one-third of the candidates who filed to run for Congress are millennials or members of Gen Z, according to On the Rise , a new analysis from Future Caucus, the organization I lead. In 2022, it was one in six. Millennials now outnumber every other generation in Senate races.

This surge of younger candidates is no mystery. Only about 10 to 15 percent of Americans approve of Congress, and roughly eight in 10 people of all parties support age limits for its members. Of the 11 incumbents who lost their primaries this year, six were defeated by younger challengers, three of whom were under 35 years old — for example, 29-year-old Melat Kiros, who defeated 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado .

Young Americans aren’t just demanding change from the sidelines — they’re volunteering to create it themselves. As one millennial state legislator told me , “I got mad. So instead of continuing to get angry, I decided to get elected.”

Running, though, is not the same as winning. The younger the candidate, the less likely they are to reach Election Day. Our research found that just 21 percent of Gen Z candidates and 30 percent of millennials made the general election ballot, compared with 41 percent of Gen Xers and 45 percent of baby boomers. In Senate races, the drop-off is steeper still.

One possible explanation? The new generation is testing party lines. Mirroring the growing independence of Gen Z voters , Gen Z candidates are the most likely to run outside the two major parties. One in six filed as a third-party or unaffiliated candidate, most of them as independents. While it may be impacting candidates’ chances for now, parties that want the next generation’s talent should read that as a warning.

The surest path to the ballot runs through the statehouse, but very few young candidates are taking it. About two in three current and former state legislators who ran for Congress this year made it to the general election, compared with about one in three of those who have never served. Yet only 9 percent of millennial candidates and fewer than 2 percent of Gen Z candidates have that experience.

That edge matters more than ever. After mid-decade redistricting, a full 85 percent of House races are rated safe for one party. That means in most districts, the primary is the real contest, and knowing how to navigate filing deadlines, petition signatures and local coalitions counts.

It matters after Election Day, too. Nearly half of today’s Congress started in a statehouse, where lawmakers learn to write a bill, count votes and work with people who see the world differently. The Center for Effective Lawmaking found that members of state Future Caucuses — bipartisan groups of young legislators — are 24 percent more effective at advancing legislation than comparable lawmakers in other states. Not only can serving at the state level help aspiring congressional candidates win, it can also help them govern.

I know “serve in your statehouse first” can sound a lot like “wait your turn,” but it isn’t. Most state legislators serve part time, keep their day jobs and win by knocking on doors. It is about as far from the Washington establishment as elected office gets.

But still, a younger candidate pool isn’t automatically a more representative one. Men outnumber women about three to one among congressional candidates today. Among Gen Z, more than four in five candidates are men — the widest gap of any generation. Even among challengers with state legislative experience, men outnumber women nearly three to one.

We can’t assume generational change will fix this on its own. Our research on why state lawmakers leave office points to forces that also keep people from running in the first place, like threats to their families’ safety, low pay, thin staff support and partisanship that makes problem-solving harder. Those forces fall hardest on women, and all of them are fixable.

Our political parties should recruit young people, especially young women, for city councils, school boards and statehouses — not just because local politics still matters deeply, but also because these offices are the surest route to a Congress that works. We should pay state legislators enough to ensure that service isn’t reserved only for those who can afford it. We must treat threats against public officials as the crimes they are.

Whoever wins in November, the bench is deep, and it is young. Let’s make sure it arrives ready to govern.

Layla Zaidane is president and CEO of Future Caucus, a nonpartisan organization for Gen Z and millennial lawmakers.

articles.title: Leavitt opens up on helping Trump find new press secretary after Zacharia debacle: 'Was not for her'
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt says she's helping Trump find a new press secretary after Katie Zacharia lasted just five days in the demanding White House role.
articles.body: MANCHESTER, N.H. - Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says she is helping President Donald Trump choose his next press secretary after his first pick for the job lasted just five days. "I've offered my help to the president to help him select someone who can serve him and the country well," Leavitt said Wednesday evening in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital. Leavitt served as Trump's press secretary from the start of the president's second term until Aug. 27, when she stepped down from the demanding role to spend more time with her two young children, including a daughter who was born in May. Her successor, political commentator Katie Zacharia, took over earlier this month, but lasted just five days in the role, making her the shortest-serving White House press secretary in U.S. history. TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF A JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT "White House press secretary is a tough job. I know that because I did it, obviously for almost two years, and many people say it's one of the hardest jobs in politics," Leavitt emphasized. She noted that the job "takes a lot of preparation and sometimes you don't know how someone will perform until they go out there." "We wish Katie the best. The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well," Leavitt added. When it comes to whom Trump will choose next for the position, Leavitt said the president "is continuing to look over options. There's a lot of people who want that job. It's an amazing job. It provides you with incredible opportunities." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Asked what advice she's offered to Trump, Leavitt said, "I'll keep my private counsel to the president private, but I do obviously talk to him about what the job entails, and he knows it very well." "Nobody understands the press better than Donald Trump. He knows he needs someone who is tough, who is smart, who understands his policies, who is loyal, and who can go out there and put up a fight," she added. Leavitt, a New Hampshire native, served as an intern in the Trump White House after graduating from Saint Anselm College in 2019. She later became an assistant White House press secretary at the end of Trump's first term. After Trump's defeat in the 2020 presidential election, Leavitt worked as communications director for Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York. She then served as spokeswoman for the Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc. before taking over as press secretary for Trump's 2024 presidential campaign. After being named White House press secretary following the 2024 election, Leavitt made history as the youngest person ever in the role. Chris Pappas. Asked if she might make another run for public office in her home state when Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan is up for re-election in 2028, Leavitt quickly said, "No, I'm all set. I don't have any plans to run for office in the near future at all, or in the future at all." articles.title: Sabato’s Crystal Ball moves Ohio governor race toward Acton after Ramaswamy attack ad
articles.summary: Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved its ratings of Ohio’s gubernatorial race toward Democratic nominee Amy Acton, following a controversial campaign ad launched by her opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy (R). Previously, the forecaster rated the race as a “toss-up,” but it has changed it to “leans Democratic,” following what it called “an explosive—and desperate—attack ad,” according…
articles.body:
Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved its ratings of Ohio’s gubernatorial race toward Democratic nominee Amy Acton, following a controversial campaign ad launched by her opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy (R).

Previously, the forecaster rated the race as a “toss-up,” but it has changed it to “leans Democratic,” following what it called “an explosive—and desperate—attack ad,” according to its Thursday report .

The clip that began circulating earlier this week features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling the Democrat “a liar” and urging Ohioans to vote against her. Initially, it was unclear who was behind the video, but Ramaswamy’s team later confirmed it was behind the ad and would spend $4 million to promote it.

In a 2019 interview with The Vindicator in Youngstown, Ohio, Acton talked about her unstable childhood where she was subject to abuse, neglect and homelessness. She opened up about facing sexual abuse at the hands of her stepfather, which resulted in criminal charges and ultimately led to her ending her relationship with her mother.

Arthur, in the video , called Acton a liar and disputed her claims of living in a tent at one point while growing up.

“She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself,” Arthur said in the video.

Acton responded Wednesday to the ad in an interview with CBS affiliate WBNS , calling it “an exploitative thing to do.”

The ad prompted widespread criticism across the board, with Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (R) telling The Associated Press on Wednesday he “would not have run” it. Husted is running for reelection against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), who said the ad was “disgusting” and called on Husted to condemn it.

“Internally, we have been giving a slight edge to Acton and Brown in our mental ledger, but we also have to continually remind ourselves that Ohio is a clearly red-leaning state,” Sabato’s Crystal Ball said.

articles.title: Slotkin's viral 'threat' to conservatives takes new twist as student moves to hold her accountable: 'Shocking'
articles.summary: Michael Bicksel, the University of Chicago student who broke the story, filed the ethics complaint arguing Elissa Slotkin's remarks targeted students.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) is facing an ethics complaint filed to the United States Senate over comments she made earlier this month that many characterized as a "threat" to conservatives who are thinking about working for the Trump administration. During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, Slotkin drew criticism after a clip went viral showing her saying she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump and push a "deterrence message" for young people. "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.' I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that,'" she said. "I want that deterrence message sent," Slotkin said. Slotkin is now facing an ethics complaint filed Thursday by Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student who first reported her remarks. The complaint was submitted to the Senate Select Committee on Ethics and argues that Slotkin proposed using congressional investigations and potential prosecutions to frighten young people away from serving in a Republican administration. FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS "Recently at an event at my college, the University of Chicago, Senator Slotkin laid out a legislative-oversight agenda that involved using the legal process to terrorize members of the Trump administration in order to âdeterâ young people from going to work for it," Bicksel wrote. The complaint asks the committee to determine whether Slotkin's comments amounted to "improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate," a standard described in the Senate Ethics Manual as applying to conduct that may be unethical even if it does not violate a specific law or Senate rule. "As a college student and a conservative, this was a shocking thing to hear," Bicksel's complaint reads. "A prominent U.S. Senator came to my college and laid out a goal that I and my peers should be afraid to serve our country in the executive branch. This is well below the standard of conduct expected of a U.S. Senator and deserves investigation by the Senate Select Committee on Ethics and appropriate subsequent disciplinary action." ELISSA SLOTKIN TELLS STUDENTS LIKE ME NOT TO WORK IN GOVERNMENT. DON'T LISTEN TO HER Bicksel argued that Slotkin's comments were directed at students considering government service, rather than exclusively at people who commit crimes or engage in unethical conduct. "The substance of the âdeterrence messageâ is clear as day," Bicksel wrote. "Her target was âyoung people coming out of schoolâ (like me and my classmates) who are debating whether they should âgo work for the Trump administration.â" "We are obviously not debating â as she subsequently tried to clarify â whether to go commit crimes or behave unethically," he continued. "Those who commit crimes should be punished for doing so. No one disagrees with that. All we are debating is public service, pure and simple, and Senator Slotkin says we should think twice about doing so because it might provoke the full power of the United States Senate." Slotkin, when pressed on the response to her comment on CNN, referred to the controversy as "manufactured outrage." "My parents were worried, you know. It's really messy. I'm not sure what to get involved in.' Politics, in general, has become messy." The Justice Department is currently facing calls to investigate Slotkin over her remarks, Washington Examiner reported on Wednesday. Slotkin's communication director pointed Fox News Digital to a statement made by the senator on Tuesday when reached for comment. "Now, if you take a breath, this is all pretty crazy. "His supporters use a coordinated play to threaten, intimidate, and silence anyone who speaks up. It's a play to distract us from his failed economy, high gas prices, and the disastrous war he started with Iran. But if I've learned one thing from this past year, it's that you have to push back."

articles.title: DeWine calls on Ramaswamy to take down ad featuring Acton’s mother
articles.summary: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) called on Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to take down an ad featuring his opponent Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother. “The ad is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine told reporters outside the Ohio Statehouse, according to The Statehouse News Bureau. “But when you know the rest of the story, when you know the…
articles.body:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) called on Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to take down an ad featuring his opponent Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother.

“The ad is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine told reporters outside the Ohio Statehouse, according to The Statehouse News Bureau . “But when you know the rest of the story, when you know the back story, when you know that the husband of the mom was indicted by a grand jury after hearing testimony and that he took off along with the mother, and that the two children never saw the mother after that. When you know that it, just to me, makes it more serious. It makes it just more wrong.”

“It’s wrong to run this ad. … I would urge Ramaswamy’s campaign to take this down,” he concluded.

A journalist followed up with DeWine, asking if he would revoke his endorsement of Ramaswamy over the ad.

“I’m not changing the endorsement. I endorse the whole ticket,” the term-limited Ohio governor said.

The ad, which is airing in Ohio, shows Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a “liar” and insinuating she suffered from mental health issues. The ad does not provide any context about the estrangement between Acton and her mother; she was taken out of Arthur’s custody at the age of 12.

Acton has talked about experiencing physical and sexual abuse, along with neglect, during her childhood. Her mother stayed with her stepfather after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old, according to court documents. Acton says the last time she saw her mother was in court the day her stepfather was taken into custody.

She has called the ad “ despicable ” and added it was “an exploitative thing to do.”

Ramaswamy took credit for the ad Tuesday, with his campaign reportedly spending $4 million on ad spots statewide. In a statement to The Associated Press, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy’s campaign said Acton’s mother was not paid for the one-minute spot.

Vice President Vance came to Ramaswamy’s defense, saying at a campaign rally that the ad “calls it out like it is,” despite multiple GOP lawmakers decrying the ad as offensive .

One of those lawmakers was outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), who on Wednesday in a CNN interview called the ad “shameful” and predicted it would hurt GOP candidates up and down the ballot in Ohio.

“This ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season,” Mace said. “The bar is low, and somehow, Vivek Ramaswamy somehow managed to limbo under the lowest bar of decency in this country.”
