articles.title: Judge directs Trump to sit for deposition in his $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC
articles.summary: A federal judge in Florida on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11 or face the possibility of having his $10 billion action dismissed.
articles.body: A federal judge in Florida on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11 or face the possibility of having his $10 billion action dismissed. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett handed down the order after the BBC’s lawyers complained that Trump was stalling. He was supposed to sit for a deposition on Oct. 16 but canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” BBC attorney Charles Tobin told the judge that matter turned out to be a political rally and a fundraiser. “He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said. Trump’s attorneys had proposed postponing his deposition until late January, which Tobin said was too late. Discovery in the case is supposed to close on Dec. 18, and Trump is the single most important witness in the case since he’s the one who claims he suffered billions of dollars in damages from the BBC’s story, Tobin said. Lett also ruled that the deposition can be videotaped —something Trump attorney Alejandro Brito argued against. The BBC declined comment. The White House referred a request for comment to a representative for Trump’s personal legal team, who did not immediately respond. Trump filed suit against the British news organization last year, alleging it aired a “false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction” of him in a documentary that spliced together comments from his speech at the Ellipse ahead of the Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021. The BBC has acknowledged splicing comments from the speech together, but maintains Trump was not defamed and that he did not suffer any damages. The BBC issued a subpoena to Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club for information on whether membership applications and fees were affected by its documentary, which did not air in the U.S. Brito had argued that subpoena should be quashed because Trump is not arguing the show impacted the business. Tobin countered that Trump’s suit says the documentary “injured President Trump in his profession, occupation and trade,” so that information should be fair game. Lett agreed that it “falls within” the kind of information that should be turned over.

Trump must be deposed by BBC lawyers before Dec. 11, U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ruled, according to The Associated Press, or face sanctions up to…
articles.body:
A federal judge ordered President Trump to be deposed as part of his lawsuit against the BBC over a documentary he says defamed him with how it was edited.

Trump must be deposed by BBC lawyers before Dec. 11, U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ruled, according to The Associated Press , or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit.

Lawyers for the president have sought in recent weeks to delay any testimony from the president, saying it notified the BBC legal team the “Plaintiff would make himself available for a deposition in the second or third week of January 2027.”

The president was previously scheduled to sit for a deposition on Oct. 16 until the BBC said Trump’s attorneys informed them “the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance.”

Trump is suing the BBC for $10 billion over the way it edited a documentary about his efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

The president is shown giving a speech rallying his supporters before the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, but the BBC omitted comments he gave telling the crowd to march “peacefully and patriotically” to the Capitol that day.

articles.title: The debt blob will destroy America
articles.summary: Citizens Against Government Waste released its 2026 edition of Prime Cuts, proposing hundreds of recommendations to reduce the national debt and eliminate wasteful federal spending.
articles.body:
Every October, Americans look for a good scare, like haunted houses and horror movies. But the most frightening phenomenon in 2026 is the monstrous national debt. This quickly growing blob is consuming everything in its path and will destroy America if it is not stopped by eliminating the waste, fraud, abuse, mismanagement, and overspending that has overtaken Washington.

On Aug. 18, 2026, the national debt topped $40 trillion for the first time, an increase of 100.8 percent from the $19.95 trillion owed when President Trump’s first term began in January 2017. That is more than $116,000 for every man, women and child in America.

If that doesn’t raise the hair on the back of your neck, the forecast will. A Feb. 17, 2026, Congressional Budget Office report projected annual deficits increasing from $1.9 trillion in fiscal 2026 to $3.1 trillion in fiscal 2036. Over this ten-year period, deficits will average $2.44 trillion a year, adding $24.4 trillion and pushing gross federal debt to $64.6 trillion by fiscal 2036, 61.5 percent more than today. The fiscal 2036 debt would equal 120 percent of GDP, eclipsing the previous record of 106 percent set in 1946.

Unlike in 1946, America is not recovering from a catastrophic world war. This debt is the result of a collective failure by the executive and legislative branches to root out waste, fraud, abuse, and mismanagement. As the horror movie trope goes, the call is coming from inside the house.

Interest payments on the national debt show this monstrosity most vividly. These payments are now the third-largest federal expenditure, behind only Social Security and Medicare, and ahead of the defense budget. Every dollar spent servicing yesterday’s borrowing is a dollar unavailable for any other purpose. No silver bullet will save future generations from paying for the sins of Americans past.

Fortunately, the debt blob can be stopped. On Oct. 14, 2026, Citizens Against Government Waste released its 2026 edition of Prime Cuts . First published in 1993, when the national debt was a mere $4.4 trillion, its 494 recommendations, drawn from proposals, both Democratic and Republican administrations and members of Congress, and nonpartisan sources, would save $639 billion in the first year and $5.6 trillion over five years.

The first item to face the waste cutting guillotine should be the Market Access Program, which helps agricultural producers promote U.S. products overseas. This blatant example of corporate welfare funnels millions to large, profitable corporations and trade associations that can afford their own advertising. Its elimination saves $907 million over five years.

Consider next the Essential Air Service , which was launched in 1978 as a temporary 10-year program to preserve rural air connections after deregulation. Nearly half a century later, this zombie program continues to shuffle along, subsidizing mostly empty flights that sometimes cost thousands of dollars per passenger for communities located a short drive from major airports. Burying the program for good would save $3.8 billion over five years.

Then there is the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, created in 2010 in the Affordable Care Act to test new payment models for Medicare, Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program. It has delivered only curses and misery. The Congressional Budget Office had projected it would save $2.8 billion between 2011 and 2020; instead, it cost taxpayers $5.4 billion, with another $1.3 billion in projected losses through 2030. Only six of its 50 models met the criteria for nationwide expansion, an abominable 12 percent success rate. After 16 years, Congress should lay that program to rest, saving taxpayers $4.1 billion over five years.

These are just a few sample offerings of cuts that should be laid on the funeral pyre of wasteful spending.

Halloween is on the last day of the first month of fiscal 2027. Elected officials in the nation’s capital can keep covering their eyes and hope the fiscal blob oozes away, or they can finally wake up and start cutting the massive government waste, fraud, abuse and mismanagement to prevent the destruction of America.

Deborah Collier is vice president of policy and government affairs at the Citizens Against Government Waste.

articles.title: The 2026 midterms are just 12 days away. Which party has a better chance of winning? Here's what the latest polls say.
articles.summary: Trump's approval rating is going down. Democrats' lead on the generic ballot is going up. Could this be a "wave" election?
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections are just 12 days away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data.

The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections. And polls have been wrong before .

Yet time is running out — and the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too.

The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally firming up — and some clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears.

Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds).

You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading.

At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.9 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House.

At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.3 points on the generic ballot. Two weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House.

Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But by late October, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively.

So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — more than 9 percentage points , on average — and it has been steadily growing over the last month.

Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House.

National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow:

What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 4 percentage points . One recent poll shows a tie.

What the latest polls say: Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7 percentage points — over the last month.

What the latest polls say : Marshall leads by 1 point in the latest sounding — but it's the only survey conducted over the last month that shows him ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points).

Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July)

Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate)

What the latest polls say : Graham holds a narrow lead in recent surveys . But it is small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well.

Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong.

Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability

To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle.

At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them.

According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 60.6% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 36.3% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -24.3% — down two points from last week, and an all-time low.

Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters:

Again, history can provide perspective . In mid-September 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November.

According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 73% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 48-point gap.

In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection.

articles.title: El debate entre Feijóo y Sánchez ya tiene fecha confirmada y será en una televisión privada
articles.standfirst: RTVE se encargaría de la contienda a cuatro entre PP, PSOE, VOX y Frente Amplio
articles.summary: RTVE se encargaría de la contienda a cuatro entre PP, PSOE, VOX y Frente Amplio
articles.body: Apenas queda un mes para que los españoles vayamos a la urnas, y los partidos ya han comenzado su campaña electoral. Al haber adelantado los comicios, lo cierto es que las diferentes formaciones se han tomado estos poco más de 30 días con mucha fuerza. Los ataques, reproches y correcciones de un lado a otro son continuos. Uno de los asuntos que quedaba por resolver era el de los debates electorales. Son muchas las cadenas las que se habían propuesto: RTVE, Antena 3 y Telecinco. También el canal de YouTube de Jordi Wild. De momento, ya sabemos que el cara a cara entre Feijóo y Sánchez va a ser en una cadena privada. Y ya hay fecha para ello: el lunes 16 de noviembre. El PSOE ha confirmado la fecha después de que el PP lo hiciera previamente. Así pues, Antena 3 o Telecinco serán los elegidos para el cara a cara. De este modo, los socialistas reiteran que no van a “vetar” a ninguna cadena privada, pero tampoco van a “consentir bajo ningún concepto” un posible veto a la pública. Del mismo modo, el PSOE ha aceptado la invitación de RTVE a participar en un debate a cuatro el jueves 26 de noviembre. El problema es que el Partido Popular había expresado su deseo de que este debate a cuatro también se llevase a cabo en una cadena privada. La postura del partido socialista hace pensar que, finalmente, ambos darán su brazo a torcer para colmar las exigencias del otro. Hay que recordar que también se exploró la posibilidad de un debate entre los distintos portavoces de estos cuatro grupos parlamentarios. Por ahora, se han confirmado dos fechas. Falta por saber si el PP aceptará el debate a cuatro en RTVE y cuál es la cadena privada elegida para el debate a dos.

articles.title: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine calls on Vivek Ramaswamy to take down ad featuring opponent’s estranged mother
articles.summary: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine is calling for Vivek Ramaswamy to stop airing an ad that features the estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.
articles.body: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine is calling for Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican he endorsed to succeed him as governor, to stop airing an ad that features the estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. “The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine said in a Thursday news conference he called to address what has become a boiling controversy in the final days of a hostile race. DeWine, however, reaffirmed his support for Ramaswamy. “Look, today is about the ad, but I’m not — no, I’m not changing my endorsement,” DeWine said when pressed by reporters at the Ohio Statehouse. “I endorse the whole ticket, as you know. I’m a Republican. I endorse the whole ticket. On that ticket are some amazing people, almost all of whom I have worked with in the past.” The Ramaswamy campaign ad, backed by a $4 million purchase of statewide airtime, features Donna Arthur, who in the minute-long spot calls her daughter a “liar” and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton has talked about being sexually abused by her mother’s husband as a child. Her brother, Philip Stearns, has corroborated her account, saying in a video for Acton’s campaign that their “birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.” Acton has said that she has not seen or spoken to her mother in nearly 50 years. Arthur has not responded to requests for comment from NBC News. The abuse claims are not referenced in the ad. But DeWine on Thursday talked about prosecuting sexual assault cases earlier in his career in public service and said that he found the ad troubling given the family history. “When you know the rest of the story, when you know the backstory, when you know that the husband of the mom was indicted by a grand jury after hearing testimony, and that he took off along with the mother … and that two children never saw, I guess, the mother after that — when you know that, it just to me makes it more serious,” DeWine said. “It makes it just more wrong.” He added: “So it’s wrong to run this ad, and even at this late time — my wife, Fran, saw the ad run this morning on TV — I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.” DeWine joins a growing list of Republicans who have condemned an ad that has been criticized on both sides of the political aisle. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, said Wednesday that he “would not have run that ad.” But there also has been a split in the Republican Party. Others, including Vice President JD Vance, whose old Senate seat Husted was appointed to last year, have downplayed the outrage over the spot. “Politics is a tough business, and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days,” Vance told reporters Wednesday in Cincinnati. Asked about Vance’s remarks Thursday, Dewine said, “Look, I’m not going to comment on what someone else said.” “I mean, this is Mike DeWine, with my life experiences, saying what I think about this ad,” he added. “So I’m going to keep it just to that.” DeWine’s life experiences aside, his willingness to reprimand Ramaswamy is not entirely surprising. He worked closely with Acton when she served as the governor’s health director during the early days of the Covid pandemic. DeWine has defended her against attacks from Ramaswamy and his allies on her leadership during that crisis. DeWine also was not initially sold on Ramaswamy’s candidacy for governor. He had originally wanted Husted, who served as his lieutenant governor, to be his successor. And last year he expressed interest in his new lieutenant governor, former Ohio State football coach Jim Tressel, challenging Ramaswamy in the Republican primary. Tressel passed, and DeWine eventually backed Ramaswamy. Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck noted that DeWine on Thursday also expressed concern over how Acton’s campaign has mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother in its messaging. DeWine also emphasized that it was Ramaswamy’s attack that had a $4 million push behind it. “Governor DeWine is correct that the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton,” Luck said. “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards when Democrats have regularly used family members of President Trump, RFK Jr., and other Republicans in ads. Voters shouldn’t buy it.”

articles.title: Biden-appointed judge blocks voter-fraud probes in battleground states just days before midterms
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled the Department of Homeland Security must halt noncitizen voting probes, citing voter intimidation from armed agents at homes.
articles.body: A Biden-appointed federal judge in California ruled Wednesday that the Department of Homeland Security must halt certain investigations into suspected illegal voting, citing concerns over voter intimidation. U.S. District Judge Araceli MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n, the jurist in question, was born in Mexico and nominated to the federal bench by President Joe Biden in 2022. Before becoming a federal judge, MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n spent about six years at the American Civil Liberties Union, a progressive civil rights organization, where she worked on women's and immigrants' rights issues. The activist groups suing DHS "demonstrate[d] that they are likely to succeed in their claim that Defendants have run afoul of the Voting Rights Actâs prohibition of intimidating voter assistance and mobilization," according to MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n. DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS The publicâs "interests in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed (the governmentâs) purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens," she added. The Trump administration, meanwhile, maintained that noncitizen voting in federal elections is a crime and that DHS has statutory authority to investigate suspected violations. MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n did not find investigating noncitizen voting as itself unlawful, but instead argued that DHSâ methods likely violate the law as it used unreliable source data and sent armed agents to homes to conduct interviews, which could constitute intimidation. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS Lawyers representing the federal government conceded that some American citizens may have been looked at in connection with DHSâ investigations, but contended that in-person interviews were "expressly designed to resolve the discrepancies." Noncitizen voting is rare, but cases of illegal voting have been documented. News broke earlier this year, for example, that New Jersey erroneously placed over 6,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls. The Justice Department announced charges against 16 individuals in September, including noncitizens accused of voting illegally in federal elections, and brought additional election-related charges in October. NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­nâs order blocks DHS from carrying out certain field investigations into suspected illegal voting involving U.S. citizens in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Several of those states are led by Democrats who have opposed the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies, and some face high-profile elections in November. Cracking down on illegal voting has been a priority for the second Trump administration, though it has yet to produce evidence of widespread noncitizen voting. The judge delayed enforcement of her order until Friday, giving the Trump administration time to appeal, and set the restrictions to expire on Election Day unless otherwise ordered. articles.title: Raj BJP launches statewide campaign to counter Cong on SIR
articles.summary: Rajasthan BJP launches 15-day “Save Democracy, Remove Mobocracy” campaign (Oct 22–Nov 5) to counter Congress on SIR, electoral roll integrity and infiltration.
articles.body: Jaipur: Rajasthan BJP Thursday announced a 15-day statewide campaign titled “Save Democracy, Remove Mobocracy” to push back against the Congress narrative on Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, voter list integrity and alleged illegal infiltration. The campaign will run from Oct 22 to Nov 5.The party said it will organise district headquarters foot marches, assembly constituency-level “Rashtra Chintan Samvad” discussions, youth interactions at educational institutions, student competitions, press conferences and social media outreach to build public awareness around electoral processes, citizenship and democratic institutions.BJP state general secretary Shravan Singh Bagri said, “Congress attempted to mislead people on SIR and other issues. The campaign would counter these allegations while highlighting the need for accurate electoral rolls, voting rights for eligible citizens and public confidence in democratic institutions.”“The country’s citizens alone have the right to vote. Infiltrators should not have the right to choose the country’s govt,” Bagri said, alleging Congress was spreading misinformation over the removal of names of non-citizens from electoral rolls.According to the party, the campaign has eight components: press conferences, district-level foot marches, Rashtra Chintan Samvad, youth interactions, student competitions, anti-infiltration publicity, special publications and social media outreach.From Oct 23 to 31, BJP said it will hold “Rashtra Chintan Samvad” programmes in every assembly constituency, involving doctors, lawyers, teachers, professors, businesspeople, social workers and other professionals.Youth dialogues are planned in colleges, universities, industrial training institutes and other educational institutions on democracy, citizenship, SIR, constitutional values, electoral fairness and national development, alongside student competitions on related themes.The party said it will also circulate articles, booklets, pamphlets and special publications, while digital platforms will carry campaign messages and updates from district-level activities.Suman Sharma, convener of the “Remove Infiltrators, Save Democracy” segment, said, “The campaign would operate at state, district and assembly constituency levels.
